Algebraic solutions of linear differential equations:
an arithmetic approach

Alin Bostan Note: Inria, Université Paris-Saclay, 1 rue Honoré d’Estienne d’Orves, 91120 Palaiseau, France.    Xavier Caruso Note: CNRS; Université de Bordeaux, IMB; Inria Bordeaux Sud-Ouest, CANARI, 351 cours de la Libération, 33405 Talence, France.    Julien Roques Note: Université de Lyon, Universite Claude Bernard Lyon 1, CNRS UMR 5208, Institut Camille Jordan, 43 Bd du 11 Novembre 1918, 69622 Villeurbanne, France.
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Given a linear differential equation with coefficients in ℚ⁡(x)\mathbb{Q}(x), an important question is to know whether its full space of solutions consists of algebraic functions, or at least if one of its specific solutions is algebraic. After presenting motivating examples coming from various branches of mathematics, we advertise in an elementary way a beautiful local-global arithmetic approach to these questions, initiated by Grothendieck in the late sixties. This approach has deep ramifications and leads to the still unsolved Grothendieck-Katz pp-curvature conjecture.

1 Context, motivation and basic examples

In this text we consider linear differential equations (LDEs) of order rr

ar​(x)​y(r)​(x)+ar−1​(x)​y(r−1)​(x)+⋯+a1​(x)​y′​(x)+a0​(x)​y​(x)=0,a_{r}(x)y^{(r)}(x)+a_{r-1}(x)y^{(r-1)}(x)+\cdots+a_{1}(x)y^{\prime}(x)+a_{0}(x)y(x)=0, (1)

where the aia_{i}’s are known rational functions in ℚ⁡(x)\mathbb{Q}(x), with ara_{r} not identically zero and y⁡(x)y(x) is an unknown “function”. In many applications, the desired solution y⁡(x)y(x) is a formal power series with coefficients in ℚ\mathbb{Q}. Therefore, in what follows, when we write “function” we actually mean an element of ℚ⁡[[x]]\mathbb{Q}[[x]] unless otherwise specified. We will say that a function y∈ℚ⁡[[x]]y\in\mathbb{Q}[[x]] is differentially finite (in short, D-finite) if it satisfies a linear differential equation like (1).

A function y∈ℚ⁡[[x]]y\in\mathbb{Q}[[x]] is called algebraic if it is algebraic over ℚ⁡(x)\mathbb{Q}(x), that is, if y⁡(x)y(x) satisfies a polynomial equation of the form P⁡(x,y⁡(x))=0P(x,y(x))=0, for some P∈ℚ⁡[x,y]∖{0}.P\in\mathbb{Q}[x,y]\setminus\{0\}. Otherwise, y⁡(x)y(x) is called transcendental. The simplest algebraic functions are polynomials in ℚ⁡[x]\mathbb{Q}[x], closely followed by rational power series: these are rational functions in ℚ⁡(x)\mathbb{Q}(x) that have no pole at x=0x=0 and therefore admit a Taylor expansion around the origin. A little more general are NN-th roots of rational power series, such as y⁡(x)=1/1−xNy(x)=1/\sqrt[N]{1-x}. In all these three cases, y⁡(x)y(x) is clearly D-finite and satisfies a linear differential equation of order r=1r=1.

Many other examples of interesting functions that might or might not be solutions of linear differential equations arise from combinatorics. A basic example is given by the Catalan numbers.

Example 1.1 (Catalan numbers).

By definition, a Dyck path is a path drawn in the quarter plane ℕ2\mathbb{N}^{2} that starts at (0,0)(0,0), consists of steps ↗\nearrow (directed by the vector (1,1)(1,1)) or ↘\searrow (directed by the vector (1,−1)(1,-1)) and finally ends on the xx-axis (see Figure 1).

Let CnC_{n} be the number of Dyck paths ending at (2​n,0)(2n,0); we say that such paths have length nn. For instance C1=1C_{1}=1 since there is a single Dyck path ending at (2,0)(2,0), namely ↗\nearrow–↘\searrow, while C2=2C_{2}=2 since there are two Dyck paths ending at (4,0)(4,0), namely ↗\nearrow–↗\nearrow–↘\searrow–↘\searrow and ↗\nearrow–↘\searrow–↗\nearrow–↘\searrow. We use the convention that C0=1C_{0}=1. We notice that any Dyck path of length n+1n+1 can be written uniquely as the concatenation of (1) a step ↗\nearrow, (2) a Dyck path of length k−1k{-}1 (translated by (1,1)(1,1)), (3) a step ↘\searrow and (4) a Dyck path of length n−kn{-}k. It follows that the sequence (Cn)n≥0(C_{n})_{n\geq 0} satisfies the following nonlinear recurrence relation:

Cn=∑k=1nCk−1​Cn−k,for all ​n≥1.C_{n}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}C_{k-1}C_{n-k},\qquad\text{for all }n\geq 1.

If y⁡(x)y(x) denotes the generating function of the CnC_{n}’s, i.e. y⁡(x)=∑n=0∞Cn​xny(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}C_{n}x^{n}, the previous relation translates to the algebraic identity

y⁡(x)=1+x⋅y​(x)2y(x)=1+x{\cdot}y(x)^{2} (2)

(the summand 11 comes from the fact that C0=1C_{0}=1). Therefore y⁡(x)y(x) is algebraic and one can even solve equation (2) and get the closed formula y⁡(x)=1−1−4​x2​xy(x)=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4x}}{2x}. It is worth noting that, starting from the algebraic relation (2), one can also derive a linear differential equation satisfied by y⁡(x)y(x). Indeed differentiating (2), one gets y′​(x)=y​(x)2+2​x​y​(x)​y′​(x)y^{\prime}(x)=y(x)^{2}+2x\>y(x)\>y^{\prime}(x). Therefore:

y′​(x)=y​(x)21−2​x​y​(x).y^{\prime}(x)=\frac{y(x)^{2}}{1-2x\>y(x)}.

The right hand side in the latter expression can be further simplified using again equation (2). Indeed notice that

(1−2​x​y​(x))2=1−4​x​y​(x)+4​x2​y​(x)2=1−4​x\big(1-2x\>y(x)\big)^{2}=1-4x\>y(x)+4x^{2}\>y(x)^{2}=1-4x

and consequently

y​(x)21−2​x​y​(x)=y​(x)2⋅(1−2​x​y​(x))1−4​x=(y⁡(x)−1)​(1−2​x​y​(x))x⁡(1−4​x)=2​x​y​(x)−y⁡(x)+1x⁡(1−4​x)\frac{y(x)^{2}}{1-2x\>y(x)}=\frac{y(x)^{2}\cdot\big(1-2x\>y(x)\big)}{1-4x}=\frac{\big(y(x)-1\big)\big(1-2x\>y(x)\big)}{x(1-4x)}=\frac{2x\>y(x)-y(x)+1}{x(1-4x)}

after replacing two times y​(x)2y(x)^{2} by y⁡(x)−1x\frac{y(x)-1}{x}.

Finally, one obtains the inhomogeneous differential equation

(4​x2−x)​y′​(x)+(2​x−1)​y​(x)+1=0.(4x^{2}-x)y^{\prime}(x)+(2x-1)y(x)+1=0.

From this, we can derive new interesting information about the sequence (Cn)n≥0(C_{n})_{n\geq 0}. For instance, it easily implies the simpler recurrence relation Cn=4​n−2n+1⋅Cn−1C_{n}=\frac{4n-2}{n+1}\cdot C_{n-1} for all n≥1n\geq 1, from which we further derive the closed formula Cn=1n+1​(2​nn)C_{n}=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}. Using Stirling’s formula, we also deduce the asymptotic estimate Cn∼4n/π​n3C_{n}\sim{4^{n}}/{\sqrt{\pi n^{3}}}.

The previous example shows that being able to write down an equation (either algebraic or differential) for a generating series can help a lot in studying its coefficients. Of course, obtaining explicit closed formulas (as we did for the Catalan numbers) will not be possible in general; however, meaningful information (such as the asymptotic growth of the coefficients) can be often extracted from the equation. Besides, in many cases it turns out that the algebraicity of a generating series is the mirror of a (sometimes hidden) “algebraic” structure on the combinatorial side which often takes the form of a recursive tree structure: in Example 1.1, for instance, a Dyck path can be decomposed as a concatenation of smaller Dyck paths which themselves can be decomposed similarly, etc. We refer to [25] for a much more detailed discussion on this topic (including much more examples).

In Example 1.1, we transformed an algebraic equation into a differential equation. It is actually a general fact and an old result, already known by Abel, that any algebraic function is D-finite. Precisely, if y⁡(x)y(x) satisfies an algebraic equation P⁡(x,y⁡(x))=0P(x,y(x))=0 with PP of degree nn in yy, then y⁡(x)y(x) also satisfies a differential equation like (1) of order rr bounded from above by nn. This follows easily from the following reasoning. By differentiating P⁡(x,y⁡(x))=0P(x,y(x))=0 with respect to xx and by using the chain rule, we obtain the equality

Px​(x,y⁡(x))+y′​(x)​Py​(x,y⁡(x))=0.P_{x}(x,y(x))+y^{\prime}(x)P_{y}(x,y(x))=0.

Here and in what follows we denote by PxP_{x} the derivative ∂P/∂x\partial P/\partial x of PP with respect to xx. Therefore, if PP is assumed to be a polynomial of minimal degree in yy satisfied by y⁡(x)y(x), then Py​(x,y​(x))P_{y}(x,y(x)) is a nonzero function in ℚ⁡[[x]]\mathbb{Q}[[x]], and hence y′(x)=−Px(x,y(x))/Py(x,y(x))y^{\prime}(x)=-P_{x}(x,y(x))/P_{y}(x,y(x)) is a rational function in y⁡(x)y(x). By using again the equation P⁡(x,y⁡(x))=0P(x,y(x))=0, it is easy to see that any rational function in y⁡(x)y(x) can be re-written as a polynomial of degree at most n−1n-1 in y⁡(x)y(x). In other terms, the derivative y′​(x)y^{\prime}(x) lives in the ℚ⁡(x)\mathbb{Q}(x)-vector space generated by 1,y⁡(x),…,y​(x)n−11,y(x),\ldots,y(x)^{n-1}. The same similarly holds for all derivatives y⁡(x),y′​(x),y′′​(x),…,y(n)​(x)y(x),y^{\prime}(x),y^{\prime\prime}(x),\ldots,y^{(n)}(x), and hence these elements must satisfy a nontrivial linear relation over ℚ⁡(x)\mathbb{Q}(x); any such relation yields a linear differential equation (1) of order at most nn. Observe that the same reasoning also proves the existence of an inhomogeneous linear differential equation of order at most n−1n-1 for y⁡(x)y(x).

A naive though very natural question is whether the converse of Abel’s result holds: is every D-finite function algebraic? The answer is negative, already for differential equations of order r=1r=1, as the following example shows.

Example 1.2.

The function exp⁡(x)≔∑n≥0xn/n!\exp(x)\coloneqq\sum_{n\geq 0}x^{n}/n!, solution of y′=yy^{\prime}=y, is transcendental. Here is a purely algebraic proof. Let us assume by contradiction that exp⁡(x)\exp(x) satisfies a polynomial equation, of minimal degree d≥1d\geq 1, of the form ed​x+∑k=0d−1rk​(x)​ek​x=0e^{dx}+\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}r_{k}(x)e^{kx}=0 for some rational functions rk​(x)∈ℚ​(x)r_{k}(x)\in\mathbb{Q}(x). By differentiating this equality with respect to xx and using exp′⁡(x)=exp⁡(x)\exp^{\prime}(x)=\exp(x), we get a new degree-dd equation d​ed​x+∑k=0d−1(rk′​(x)+k​rk​(x))​ek​x=0de^{dx}+\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}(r_{k}^{\prime}(x)+kr_{k}(x))e^{kx}=0 which by minimality is equal the former up to a factor dd. In other words, rk′​(x)+k​rk​(x)=d​rk​(x)r_{k}^{\prime}(x)+kr_{k}(x)=dr_{k}(x) for all k<dk<d. In particular, r0′​(x)=d​r0​(x)r_{0}^{\prime}(x)=dr_{0}(x), which implies that r0=0r_{0}=0. (Indeed, if r0​(x)=A/Br_{0}(x)=A/B for two coprime polynomials A,B∈ℚ⁡[x]A,B\in\mathbb{Q}[x] with A′​B−A​B′=d​A​BA^{\prime}B-AB^{\prime}=dAB, then BB divides A​B′AB^{\prime}, hence BB divides B′B^{\prime} and B′=0B^{\prime}=0. Thus A′=d​AA^{\prime}=dA, which implies A=0A=0 and r0​(x)=0r_{0}(x)=0.) The nullity of r0r_{0} now implies that exp⁡(x)\exp(x) satisfies a polynomial equation of degree d−1d-1, which contradicts the minimality of dd.

The reader could object that in Example 1.2 we were probably lucky, because the differential equation of exp⁡(x)\exp(x) is so simple, being of order 1 with constant coefficients. Indeed, in the particular case of the exponential function, there are many other ad-hoc transcendence proofs, based on various branches of mathematics. For instance, a direct analytic argument is that, viewed as a complex analytic function, any non-polynomial algebraic function needs to have a finite (and positive) radius of convergence, while exp⁡(x)\exp(x) is entire (that is, analytic in the whole complex plane). Another proof is that exp⁡(x)\exp(x) cannot satisfy a nontrivial algebraic equation, since otherwise by specializing that equation at x=1x=1 we would obtain that the number e=exp⁡(1)e=\exp(1) is an algebraic number, a statement known be to false since Hermite (1873). One could qualify this last proof as “cheating”, since it is intuitively clear that proving transcendence of functions should be easier than proving transcendence of numbers.

A systematic and very useful analytic way to establish functional transcendence is Flajolet’s criterion [46, Criterion D] (see also [47, Thm. VII.8] and [67, §2.3]). It is a consequence of the classical Newton-Puiseux theorem on fractional (Puiseux) series expansion of algebraic functions and on Darboux’s transfer results from the local behavior of f⁡(x)=∑n≥0an​xnf(x)=\sum_{n\geq 0}a_{n}x^{n} around its singularities to the asymptotic behavior of its coefficient sequence (an)n≥0(a_{n})_{n\geq 0}. Before stating it, we recall the definition of the gamma function

Γ⁡(s)≔∫0+∞ts−1​et​𝑑t,\Gamma(s)\coloneqq\int_{0}^{+\infty}t^{s-1}e^{t}dt,

where the variable ss is a complex number with positive real part. The gamma function interpolates the factorial in the sense that Γ⁡(n)=(n−1)!\Gamma(n)=(n{-}1)! for any positive integer nn.

Proposition 1.3 (Theorems A and D in [46]).

Let f⁡(x)=∑n≥0an​xn∈ℚ⁡[[x]]∖ℚ⁡[x]f(x)=\sum_{n\geq 0}a_{n}x^{n}\in\mathbb{Q}[[x]]\setminus\mathbb{Q}[x] be an algebraic non-polynomial function. Then f⁡(x)f(x) has a finite number of singularities, a finite nonzero radius of convergence, and its coefficient sequence (an)n≥0(a_{n})_{n\geq 0} is such that

an=βn​nrΓ⁡(r+1)​∑i=0mCi​ωin+O⁡(βn​nq),a_{n}=\frac{\beta^{n}n^{r}}{\Gamma(r+1)}\sum_{i=0}^{m}C_{i}\omega_{i}^{n}+O(\beta^{n}n^{q}), (3)

where m∈ℤ≥0m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, r∈ℚ∖ℤ<0r\in\mathbb{Q}\setminus\mathbb{Z}_{<0}, q<rq<r, β∈ℚ¯>0\beta\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{>0}, and Ci,ωi∈ℚ¯∖{0}C_{i},\omega_{i}\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\setminus\{0\} with |ωi|=1|\omega_{i}|=1.

The most useful form of the criterion is the following:

Corollary 1.4 (“Flajolet’s criterion”).

If f⁡(x)=∑n≥0an​xn∈ℚ⁡[[x]]f(x)=\sum_{n\geq 0}a_{n}x^{n}\in\mathbb{Q}[[x]] and an∼γ​βn​nra_{n}\sim\gamma\,\beta^{n}\,n^{r} with either r∉ℚ∖ℤ<0r\not\in\mathbb{Q}\setminus\mathbb{Z}_{<0}, or β∉ℚ¯>0\beta\notin\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{>0}, or γ⋅Γ⁡(r+1)∉ℚ¯\gamma\cdot\Gamma(r+1)\notin\overline{\mathbb{Q}}, then f⁡(x)f(x) is transcendental.

As an example of application, Proposition 1.3 immediately implies that exp⁡(x)=∑n≥0xn/n!\exp(x)=\sum_{n\geq 0}x^{n}/n! is transcendental, since the sequence 1/n!1/n! is not of the form (3) (or, since the radius of convergence of exp⁡(x)\exp(x) is infinite).

At this point, we can ask ourselves: is there a purely arithmetic proof of the transcendence of exp⁡(x)\exp(x)? This question can be seen as the starting point of the present article, whose main aim is precisely to advertise a very beautiful number-theoretic approach to algebraicity of solutions of linear differential equations. More generally, we can raise the following question.

Question 1.5.

Is there any number-theoretic way to recognize whether the differential equation (1) admits only algebraic solutions in its solution space?

Nicely enough, the answer to this question is positive, for two distinct but related reasons. Let us first explain them a bit in the case of the exponential function exp⁡(x)=∑k≥0xk/k!\exp(x)=\sum_{k\geq 0}x^{k}/k!. The first arithmetic proof of the transcendence of exp⁡(x)\exp(x) is based on the following result, which in rough terms asserts that the coefficients of algebraic functions are “almost integral”.

Proposition 1.6 (“Eisenstein’s criterion” (1852)).

If the function y⁡(x)=∑k≥0ak​xk∈ℚ⁡[[x]]y(x)=\sum_{k\geq 0}a_{k}x^{k}\in\mathbb{Q}[[x]] is algebraic, then there exists N∈ℕ∖{0}N\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\} such that y⁡(N​x)−y⁡(0)∈ℤ⁡[[x]]y(Nx)-y(0)\in\mathbb{Z}[[x]]. In particular, only a finite number of prime numbers can divide the denominators of the coefficients aka_{k}.

Since in the factorial sequence (k!)k≥0(k!)_{k\geq 0} obviously all prime numbers appear as divisors, Proposition 1.6 immediately implies that exp⁡(x)\exp(x) is transcendental.

To formulate the second arithmetic proof of the transcendence of exp⁡(x)\exp(x), we will need a little bit of additional vocabulary. The differential equation (1) can be rewritten in the compact form ℒ⁡(y)=0\mathscr{L}(y)=0, where ℒ\mathscr{L} is the linear differential operator

ℒ=ar(x)⋅∂xr+ar−1(x)⋅∂xr−1+⋯+a1(x)⋅∂x+a0(x).\mathscr{L}=a_{r}(x){\cdot}\partial_{x}^{r}+a_{r-1}(x){\cdot}\partial_{x}^{r-1}+\cdots+a_{1}(x){\cdot}\partial_{x}+a_{0}(x). (4)

We denote by ℚ(x)⟨∂x⟩\mathbb{Q}(x)\langle\partial_{x}\rangle the set of such linear differential operators. For convenience, we also allow the trivial operator, in which all coefficients ai​(x)a_{i}(x) are zero. The elements of ℚ(x)⟨∂x⟩\mathbb{Q}(x)\langle\partial_{x}\rangle act on functions in xx by letting the variable ∂x\partial_{x} act through the differentiation dd​x\frac{d}{dx}. The set ℚ(x)⟨∂x⟩\mathbb{Q}(x)\langle\partial_{x}\rangle is then endowed with a structure of noncommutative ring where the addition is the usual one but the multiplication is twisted according to the following rule, reminiscent from Leibniz’s differentiation rule:

∀r∈ℚ(x),∂xr(x)=r(x)∂x+r′(x).\forall r\in\mathbb{Q}(x),\quad\partial_{x}r(x)=r(x)\partial_{x}+r^{\prime}(x).

Although the ring ℚ(x)⟨∂x⟩\mathbb{Q}(x)\langle\partial_{x}\rangle is noncommutative, it shares many properties with the classical commutative ring of polynomials ℚ​(x)​[y]\mathbb{Q}(x)[y]. First, one has a well-defined notion of degree: the degree of the nonzero operator ℒ\mathscr{L} in (4) is the order rr of the corresponding differential equation (1), that is the largest integer rr such that ar​(x)≠0a_{r}(x)\neq 0. We will denote it by ord​(ℒ)\text{\rm ord}(\mathscr{L}) in what follows. Second, the ring ℚ(x)⟨∂x⟩\mathbb{Q}(x)\langle\partial_{x}\rangle admits an Euclidean division.

Proposition 1.7.

The ring ℚ(x)⟨∂x⟩\mathbb{Q}(x)\langle\partial_{x}\rangle is right Euclidean, i.e., for all A,B∈ℚ(x)⟨∂x⟩A,B\in\mathbb{Q}(x)\langle\partial_{x}\rangle with B≠0B\neq 0, there exist QQ and RR in ℚ(x)⟨∂x⟩\mathbb{Q}(x)\langle\partial_{x}\rangle such that A=Q​B+RA=QB+R and ord​R<ord​B\text{\rm ord}R<\text{\rm ord}B. Moreover, the pair (Q,R)(Q,R) is unique with these properties.

Using these notions, we can now formulate a very basic but important arithmetic result.

Proposition 1.8.

If all solutions of (1) are algebraic functions, then for all but a finite number of prime numbers pp, the remainder of the right Euclidean division of ∂xp\partial_{x}^{p} by ℒ\mathscr{L} has all its coefficients divisible by pp.

Proof.

By Eisenstein’s criterion (Proposition 1.6), there exists a basis of algebraic solutions y1,…,yry_{1},\ldots,y_{r} of ℒ\mathscr{L} and an integer N∈ℕ∖{0}N\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\} such that yi​(x)y_{i}(x) is in ℚ+x​ℤ​[[xN]]\mathbb{Q}+x\mathbb{Z}[[\frac{x}{N}]] for all ii. This implies that for all but a finite number of prime numbers pp (namely, the ones dividing NN and the denominators of yi​(0)y_{i}(0)) the power series yi(p)​(x)y_{i}^{(p)}(x) are in p​ℤ​[[x]]p\mathbb{Z}[[x]], i.e. zero modulo pp. Thus, writing ∂xp=Qℒ+R\partial_{x}^{p}=Q\mathscr{L}+R with RR of order at most r−1r-1, we have R⁡(yi)=0modpR(y_{i})=0\bmod p for all ii. Writing R=c0(x)+⋯+cr−1(x)∂xr−1R=c_{0}(x)+\cdots+c_{r-1}(x)\partial_{x}^{r-1}, we deduce that the vector (c0,…,cr−1)(c_{0},\ldots,c_{r-1}) times the Wronskian matrix of the yiy_{i}’s is zero modulo pp. Since the Wronskian matrix is invertible (because the yiy_{i}’s form a basis of solutions of ℒ\mathscr{L}), it is also invertible modulo pp for all but a finite number of prime numbers pp, and thus the cic_{i}’s are all 00 modulo pp for any such prime pp. ∎

Example 1.9.

The generating function of the Catalan numbers, y⁡(x)=∑k≥0Ck​xky(x)=\sum_{k\geq 0}C_{k}x^{k}, satisfies the differential equation (4​x2−x)​y′′​(x)+(10​x−2)​y′​(x)+2​y​(x)=0(4x^{2}-x)y^{\prime\prime}(x)+(10x-2)y^{\prime}(x)+2y(x)=0, which is easily deduced, either from the inhomogeneous differential equation of order 1 in Example 1.1, or directly from the recurrence (k+2)​Ck+1−(4​k+2)​Ck=0(k+2)C_{k+1}-(4k+2)C_{k}=0. The associated differential operator is ℒ=(4x2−x)∂x2+(10x−2)∂x+2\mathscr{L}=\left(4x^{2}-x\right)\partial_{x}^{2}+\left(10x-2\right)\partial_{x}+2, and the remainders of the right Euclidean divisions of ∂xp\partial_{x}^{p} by ℒ\mathscr{L} for p∈{2,3,5}p\in\{2,3,5\} are

∂x2modℒ\displaystyle\partial_{x}^{2}\bmod\mathscr{L} =−2​(5​x−1)x⁡(4​x−1)∂x−2x⁡(4​x−1),\displaystyle=-\frac{2\left(5x-1\right)}{x\left(4x-1\right)}\partial_{x}-\frac{2}{x\left(4x-1\right)},
∂x3modℒ\displaystyle\partial_{x}^{3}\bmod\mathscr{L} =6​(22​x2−9​x+1)x2​(4​x−1)2∂x+6​(6​x−1)x2​(4​x−1)2,\displaystyle=\frac{6\left(22x^{2}-9x+1\right)}{x^{2}\left(4x-1\right)^{2}}\partial_{x}+\frac{6(6x-1)}{x^{2}\left(4x-1\right)^{2}},
∂x5modℒ\displaystyle\partial_{x}^{5}\bmod\mathscr{L} =120​(386​x4−325​x3+110​x2−17​x+1)x4​(4​x−1)4∂x+120​(130​x3−69​x2+14​x−1)x4​(4​x−1)4.\displaystyle=\frac{120\left(386x^{4}-325x^{3}+110x^{2}-17x+1\right)}{x^{4}\left(4x-1\right)^{4}}\partial_{x}+\frac{120(130x^{3}-69x^{2}+14x-1)}{x^{4}\left(4x-1\right)^{4}}.

Note that indeed, we have ∂xpmodℒ=0\partial_{x}^{p}\bmod\mathscr{L}=0 modulo pp, in the three cases.

Proposition 1.8 will be discussed in more detail in §3.2. For now, let us simply observe how it implies the transcendence of exp⁡(x)\exp(x). In this case ℒ=∂x−1\mathscr{L}=\partial_{x}-1. Hence ∂xpmodℒ\partial_{x}^{p}\bmod\mathscr{L} is equal to 1 for all pp. Indeed, in this case, ℒ\mathscr{L} and ∂x\partial_{x} commute, hence the computation of the remainder is the same as the computation in ℚ⁡[x]\mathbb{Q}[x] of the remainder of xpx^{p} by x−1x-1, that is the evaluation of xpx^{p} at x=1x=1.

Example 1.10.

Let us consider the logarithmic function y⁡(x)=log⁡(1−x)y(x)=\log(1-x). Of course, since log⁡(exp⁡(x))=x\log(\exp(x))=x and exp⁡(log⁡(1−x))=1−x\exp(\log(1-x))=1-x, the transcendence of the logarithm function follows from that of the exponential function. However, the two arithmetic criteria can be used directly. First, Eisenstein’s criterion (Proposition 1.6) can be applied since log(1−x)=−∑k≥1xk/k\log(1-x)=-\sum_{k\geq 1}x^{k}/k. Second, we have that a full basis of solutions of ℒ=(1−x)∂x2−∂x\mathscr{L}=(1-x)\partial_{x}^{2}-\partial_{x} is {1,log⁡(1−x)}\{1,\log(1-x)\}, and it holds by induction that

∂xnmodℒ=(n−1)!(1−x)n−1∂xfor alln≥1.\partial_{x}^{n}\bmod\mathscr{L}=\frac{(n-1)!}{(1-x)^{n-1}}\partial_{x}\qquad\text{for all}\;n\geq 1.

Therefore, Wilson’s theorem implies that modulo any prime number pp, the remainder ∂xpmodℒ\partial_{x}^{p}\bmod\mathscr{L} is equal to −1(1−x)p−1∂x-\frac{1}{(1-x)^{p-1}}\partial_{x}, hence it is never 0. Then, Proposition 1.8 implies that log⁡(1−x)\log(1-x) is transcendental.

A natural question is whether the converses of Proposition 1.6 and Proposition 1.8 have any chance to hold true. Concerning Proposition 1.6, it is not difficult to exhibit a transcendental D-finite power series with integer coefficients, showing that its converse is false. A natural example that comes to mind is y⁡(x)=∑k≥0k!​xky(x)=\sum_{k\geq 0}k!x^{k}, which satisfies x2​y′′​(x)+(3​x−1)​y′​(x)+y⁡(x)=0x^{2}y^{\prime\prime}(x)+(3x-1)y^{\prime}(x)+y(x)=0. One can prove that y⁡(x)y(x) is not algebraic in various ways. One of them is again analytic, by observing that y⁡(x)y(x) has radius of convergence 00 and by applying Proposition 1.3. A purely algebraic proof also exists, but it is less immediate: it relies on the combination of the following facts: (i) y⁡(x)y(x) does not satisfy any first-order differential equation, hence the second-order differential equation above is the minimal-order LDE satisfied by y⁡(x)y(x); (ii) this second-order differential equation admits in its solution space the transcendental solution e−1/x/xe^{-1/x}/x; (iii) if y⁡(x)y(x) were algebraic, then its minimal-order LDE would have only algebraic solutions (Proposition 2.5 in [80]).

However, the reader may object that this counterexample is “degenerate” since the coefficient sequence (k!)k≥0(k!)_{k\geq 0} grows too fast, which is not compatible with the growth of the coefficient sequence of an algebraic function. A better converse of Proposition 1.6 would be: is there any example of a D-finite but transcendental function y∈ℤ⁡[[x]]y\in\mathbb{Z}[[x]], whose coefficient sequence grows at most geometrically? The answer is again positive.

Example 1.11.

Let again (Ck)(C_{k}) be the sequence of Catalan numbers, and consider the function y⁡(x)=∑k≥0Ck​(2​kk)​xky(x)=\sum_{k\geq 0}C_{k}\binom{2k}{k}x^{k}. One easily checks that it is D-finite and it satisfies the second-order equation x⁡(16​x−1)​y′′​(x)+2​(16​x−1)​y′​(x)+4​y​(x)=0x(16x-1)y^{\prime\prime}(x)+2(16x-1)y^{\prime}(x)+4y(x)=0. From there, it follows that y⁡(x)y(x) is the Gauss hypergeometric function F12​([1/2,1/2],[2],16​x){}_{2}F_{1}([1/2,1/2],[2];16x) and classical results (that we shall recall in §2.1.3) imply that y⁡(x)y(x) is transcendental.

Thus, even the stronger converse of Proposition 1.6 appears to be false. One may wonder if there is any way to reinforce even further the conclusion of Proposition 1.6, such that its converse becomes true. As of today, this is still an open problem, although there exist conjectural statements in this spirit. One of them is the following:

Conjecture 1.12 (Christol-André conjecture).

Assume that y⁡(x)=∑k≥0ak​xk∈ℚ⁡[[x]]y(x)=\sum_{k\geq 0}a_{k}x^{k}\in\mathbb{Q}[[x]] is D-finite. Let ℒ\mathscr{L} be the minimal-order monic linear differential equation satisfied by y⁡(x)y(x). We assume that:

  • (1)(1)

    the sequence (ak)k≥0(a_{k})_{k\geq 0} has at most geometric growth;

  • (2)(2)

    there exists N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} such that y⁡(N​x)−y⁡(0)∈ℤ⁡[[x]]y(Nx)-y(0)\in\mathbb{Z}[[x]];

  • (3)(3)

    the point x=0x=0 is not a pole of any of the coefficients of ℒ\mathscr{L}.

Then, y⁡(x)y(x) is algebraic.

If rr denotes the order of ℒ\mathscr{L}, it is also conjectured that condition (3) can be replaced by

  • (3​b)(3b)

    ℒ\mathscr{L} has rr linearly independent solutions in ℂ⁡((x1/D))\mathbb{C}((x^{1/D})) for some positive integer DD.

Now, what about the converse of Proposition 1.8? It turns out that this converse is one of the simplest formulations of what is usually called the Grothendieck conjecture. This conjecture has been formulated in the late 1960s and it has a rich history. It was proved for some important classes of differential equations (1), which will be discussed in Section 3.

Conjecture 1.13 (Grothendieck’s conjecture, version 1).

Let ℒ∈ℚ(x)⟨∂x⟩\mathscr{L}\in\mathbb{Q}(x)\langle\partial_{x}\rangle be the differential operator attached to (1). If for all but a finite number of prime numbers pp, the remainder of the right Euclidean division of ∂xp\partial_{x}^{p} by ℒ\mathscr{L} has all its coefficients divisible by pp, then all solutions of (1) are algebraic functions over ℚ⁡(x)\mathbb{Q}(x).

Example 1.14.

Consider the operator

ℒ=2x(x−1)∂x2+(4x−1)∂x+1.\mathscr{L}=2x\left(x-1\right)\partial_{x}^{2}+\left(4x-1\right)\partial_{x}+1.

Then, for any prime number p>2p>2, the reduction modulo pp of ∂xpmodℒ\partial_{x}^{p}\bmod\mathscr{L} is equal to 0 if p≡1mod4p\equiv 1\bmod 4; else, it is equal to

−2(x⁡(x−1))p−12∂x−1(x−1)p+12​xp−12.-\frac{2}{(x(x-1))^{\frac{p-1}{2}}}\partial_{x}-\frac{1}{(x-1)^{\frac{p+1}{2}}x^{\frac{p-1}{2}}}.

Therefore, for half of the primes pp, the remainder is nonzero, hence Proposition 1.8 implies that ℒ\mathscr{L} does not admit only algebraic solutions.

Example 1.15.

Consider now the operator

ℒr=2x(x−1)∂x2+(4x−1)∂x+2r(1−r),withr∈ℚ∖{1/2},\mathscr{L}_{r}=2x\left(x-1\right)\partial_{x}^{2}+\left(4x-1\right)\partial_{x}+2r(1-r),\quad\text{with}\;r\in\mathbb{Q}\setminus\{1/2\},

which is a tiny modification of the operator in Example 1.14: only the constant term has changed. Then, for any prime p≠2p\neq 2 not dividing the denominator of rr, the reduction modulo pp of ∂xpmodℒr\partial_{x}^{p}\bmod\mathscr{L}_{r} is equal to

r(r+1)⋯ (r+p−12)       ⋀       ⋯(r+p−1)(x⁡(x−1))p−12∂x+r(r+1)⋯ (r+p−12)       ⋀       ⋯(r+p−1)2​(x−1)p+12​xp−12,\frac{r(r+1)\cdots\hbox{\hskip 20.90027pt\hskip-20.90027pt\hbox{$(r+\frac{p-1}{2})$}\hskip-20.90027pt\hskip-4.16667pt\raisebox{18.50012pt}{\hbox{$\hbox{\lx@scalerel@obj{\lx@scalerel@obj{\lx@scalerel@obj{\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt}}}}$}}\hskip-4.16667pt\hskip 20.90027pt}\cdots(r+p-1)}{(x(x-1))^{\frac{p-1}{2}}}\partial_{x}+\frac{r(r+1)\cdots\hbox{\hskip 20.90027pt\hskip-20.90027pt\hbox{$(r+\frac{p-1}{2})$}\hskip-20.90027pt\hskip-4.16667pt\raisebox{18.50012pt}{\hbox{$\hbox{\lx@scalerel@obj{\lx@scalerel@obj{\lx@scalerel@obj{\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt}}}}$}}\hskip-4.16667pt\hskip 20.90027pt}\cdots(r+p-1)}{2(x-1)^{\frac{p+1}{2}}x^{\frac{p-1}{2}}},

where the notation   (r+p−12)(r+\frac{p-1}{2}) ⋀    indicates that r+p−12r+\frac{p-1}{2} is missing in the above products. For any prime number p>2p>2 not dividing the denominator of rr nor the numerator of 2​r−12r-1, the previous remainder is zero modulo pp. Therefore, for all but finitely many primes pp, the remainder is zero modulo pp.

Can we conclude that the operator ℒr\mathscr{L}_{r} admits only algebraic solutions? Conjecture 1.13 predicts that the answer is positive and, indeed, one easily checks that ℒr\mathscr{L}_{r} admits the algebraic solutions f1=(x+x−1)2​r−1/x−1f_{1}={\left(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{x-1}\right)^{2r-1}}/{\sqrt{x-1}} and f2=(x+x−1)1−2​r/x−1f_{2}={\left(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{x-1}\right)^{1-2r}}/{\sqrt{x-1}}, which are linearly independent for r≠12r\neq\frac{1}{2} since f1​f2′−f2​f1′=(1−2​r)/(x​(x−1)3/2)f_{1}f_{2}^{\prime}-f_{2}f_{1}^{\prime}=(1-2r)/(\sqrt{x}\,\left(x-1\right)^{{3}/{2}}).

2 Several natural differential equations have algebraic solutions

As we have just seen in Section 1, although in general the solutions y⁡(x)y(x) of (1) are transcendental functions (e.g., y⁡(x)=exp⁡(x)y(x)=\exp(x) and y⁡(x)=log⁡(1−x)y(x)=\log(1-x)), it may happen sometimes that they are algebraic. Most of the examples given in Section 1 were “academic examples”, in the sense that they were simple and constructed to illustrate the exposition.

The aim of this section is to give evidences showing that linear differential equations naturally appear in many areas of mathematics, including algebra, combinatorics and number theory. In all these settings, we shall see examples of differential equations that admit algebraic solutions and others that do not, demonstrating that both behaviors are common and deserve our attention. Hence, besides its beauty and intrinsic fundamental nature, being able to recognize whether a given D-finite function is algebraic or not appears as an important question, likely to have profound applications.

For instance, in number theory one often wants to understand the (algebraic or transcendental) nature of a complex number given as the value f⁡(α)f(\alpha) of a function f∈ℚ⁡[[x]]f\in\mathbb{Q}[[x]] at an algebraic point α∈ℚ¯\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}; understanding the algebraic nature of the corresponding function f⁡(x)f(x) is a first important step in this process. In the theory of the E-functions (an important class of D-finite functions generalizing the exponential function), the methods of Siegel and Shidlovskii, revisited recently in [1] and [21], are used to show that a number (such as e=exp⁡(1)e=\exp(1)) is transcendental by checking, among other things, that it is the value of a transcendental EE-function. Another motivation comes from combinatorics, where predicting the nature of the generating function of some class of combinatorial objects is a central task, as it may reveal strong underlying structures. Indeed, knowing that a class of objects is counted by an algebraic function suggests that it should be possible to construct these objects recursively by concatenation of objects of the same type [25].

2.1 Examples from Special functions: Hypergeometric functions

2.1.1 Elliptic integrals: Euler’s differential equation

Perhaps one of the oldest special functions distinct from the classical algebraic, exponential, logarithmic, or trigonometric functions, is the one arising from the question: what is the perimeter p⁡(x)p(x) of an ellipse with semi-major axis 11, as a function of its eccentricity xx? (Recall that the eccentricity is the quotient between the focal distance and the semi-major axis.)

This question, which was solved by Euler [43, §7] in 1733, is more challenging than the analogue one with “perimeter” replaced by “area”, since the area is expressible algebraically as π​1−x2\pi\sqrt{1-x^{2}}. First, we express the arc length using a real integral and the parametrization of the ellipse:

p⁡(x)=4​∫011−x2​u21−u2​d​u=2​π−π2​x2−3​π32​x4−5​π128​x6−175​π8192​x8−⋯.p(x)=4{\mathop{\text{\Large$\int_{\text{\normalsize$\scriptstyle\kern-1.63885pt0$}}^{\text{\normalsize$\scriptstyle 1$}}$}}\nolimits\sqrt{\frac{1-x^{2}u^{2}}{1-u^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}u}=2\pi-\frac{\pi}{2}x^{2}-\frac{3\pi}{32}x^{4}-\frac{5\pi}{128}x^{6}-\frac{175\pi}{8192}x^{8}-\cdots. (5)

Up to the factor of 4, the function p⁡(x)p(x) is called the complete elliptic integral of the second kind. The second equality above is obtained by expanding the integrand in power series with respect to xx, and integrating between 0 and 1. It is a fact familiar to algebraic geometers that this function p⁡(x)p(x) satisfies a linear differential equation: p⁡(x)p(x) is what we call a period function and, as such, it satisfies a linear differential equation called Picard-Fuchs differential equation (or Gauss-Manin connection). An alternative way to establish this fact and to find a differential equation satisfied by p⁡(x)p(x) is to use the “method of creative telescoping” [2]. The “magic” of creative telescoping is that it constructs the equality below, which expresses a linear combination of the integrand and of its first and second derivative with respect to xx as a pure derivative with respect to uu of another algebraic function (a rational multiple of the integrand):

((x−x3)∂x2+(1−x2)∂x+x)(1−x2​u21−u2)=∂u(x​u​1−u21−x2​u2).\left({(x-x^{3})\partial_{x}^{2}+(1-x^{2})\partial_{x}+x}\right)\left(\sqrt{\frac{1-x^{2}u^{2}}{1-u^{2}}}\right)=\partial_{u}\left(\frac{xu\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}u^{2}}}\right). (6)

Now, integrating both sides of Eq. 6 with respect to uu, it follows that p⁡(x)p(x) is a D-finite function with respect to xx, and that it satisfies the linear differential equation

(x−x3)​p′′​(x)+(1−x2)​p′​(x)+x​p​(x)=0.(x-x^{3})p^{\prime\prime}(x)+(1-x^{2})p^{\prime}(x)+xp(x)=0. (7)

Writing p⁡(x)=∑k≥0ak​xkp(x)=\sum_{k\geq 0}a_{k}x^{k}, we deduce from Eq. 7 the recursion (k−1)​(k+1)​ak=(k+2)2​ak+2(k-1)(k+1)a_{k}=(k+2)^{2}a_{k+2} for all k≥0k\geq 0. From a0=2​πa_{0}=2\pi and a1=0a_{1}=0 it follows that

a2​k=2​π​(2​kk)2(1−2​k)​16kanda2​k+1=0for all​k≥0.a_{2k}=\frac{2\pi\binom{2k}{k}^{2}}{(1-2k)16^{k}}\quad\text{and}\quad a_{2k+1}=0\quad\text{for all}\;k\geq 0.

Stirling’s formula then implies that a2​k∼−1/k2a_{2k}\sim-1/k^{2}, and hence transcendence of p⁡(x)p(x). Indeed, the presence of the factor k−2k^{-2} is incompatible with algebraicity by Flajolet’s criterion (Corollary 1.4).

2.1.2 Elliptic integrals: Legendre’s differential equation

A special function similar to p⁡(x)p(x) is obtained by a different construction. Consider the family of elliptic curves (with x∈ℂx\in\mathbb{C}) given by the Legendre equation

Ex:y2=u⁡(u−1)​(u−x).E_{x}:\qquad y^{2}=u(u-1)(u-x).

On ExE_{x}, there exists a unique (up to a constant multiple) holomorphic 1-form, given by

ωx=d​uy=d​uu​(u−1)​(u−x).\omega_{x}=\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{y}=\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\sqrt{u(u-1)(u-x)}}.

This form is necessarily closed since it is a holomorphic 1-form on a variety of complex dimension 1. The method of creative telescoping finds an exact form that is a linear combination of ωx\omega_{x} and of its first and second derivatives with respect to xx, namely

((4x2−4x)∂x2+(8x−4)∂x+1)ωx=−d(2​u⁡(u−1)(u−x)3/2).\left({(4x^{2}-4x)\partial_{x}^{2}+(8x-4)\partial_{x}+1}\right)\omega_{x}=-\mathrm{d}\left(\frac{2\sqrt{u(u-1)}}{(u-x)^{3/2}}\right). (8)

From Eq. 8 it follows that the integral y⁡(x)=∫γωxy(x)=\int_{\gamma}\omega_{x} over any closed curve γ\gamma on ExE_{x} satisfies the Legendre differential equation

(4​x2−4​x)​y′′​(x)+(8​x−4)​y′​(x)+y⁡(x)=0.(4x^{2}-4x)y^{\prime\prime}(x)+(8x-4)y^{\prime}(x)+y(x)=0. (9)

This is the most basic case of the Picard–Fuchs differential equation of a period function. For instance, by taking CC to be the curve on ExE_{x} given by the double cover y=±u​(u−1)​(u−x)y=\pm\sqrt{u(u-1)(u-x)} of [1,∞)[1,\infty), the corresponding period is the complete elliptic integral of the first kind,

∫Cωx=2​∫1∞d​uu​(u−1)​(u−x)=∑k≥0bk​xk,\mathop{\text{\large$\int_{\text{\normalsize$\scriptstyle C$}}$}}\nolimits\omega_{x}=2\mathop{\text{\large$\int_{\text{\normalsize$\scriptstyle\kern-1.22911pt1$}}^{\text{\normalsize$\scriptstyle\infty$}}$}}\nolimits\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\sqrt{u(u-1)(u-x)}}=\sum_{k\geq 0}b_{k}x^{k},

where b0=2​∫1∞d​uu​u−1=2​πb_{0}=2\mathop{\text{\Large$\int_{\text{\normalsize$\scriptstyle\kern-1.63885pt1$}}^{\text{\normalsize$\scriptstyle\infty$}}$}}\nolimits\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{u\sqrt{u-1}}=2\pi and (2​k+1)2​bk=4​(k+1)2​bk+1\left(2k+1\right)^{2}b_{k}=4\left(k+1\right)^{2}b_{k+1} for all k≥0k\geq 0, this recurrence relation being a consequence of the fact that y⁡(x)=∫Cωxy(x)=\int_{C}\omega_{x} satisfies Eq. 9. Thus,

∫Cωx=2​π​∑k≥0(2​kk)2​(x16)k.\mathop{\text{\large$\int_{\text{\normalsize$\scriptstyle C$}}$}}\nolimits\omega_{x}=2\pi\sum_{k\geq 0}\binom{2k}{k}^{2}\left(\frac{x}{16}\right)^{k}. (10)

Once again, Stirling’s formula gives bk∼2/kb_{k}\sim 2/k, which excludes algebraicity of y⁡(x)=∫Cωxy(x)=\int_{C}\omega_{x} by Flajolet’s criterion (Corollary 1.4).

2.1.3 Gauss’ hypergeometric functions

The D-finite functions considered in Sections 2.1.1 and 2.1.2 are special cases of the Gauss hypergeometric function with parameters a,b,c∈ℚa,b,c\in\mathbb{Q}, c∉ℤ≤0c\notin\mathbb{Z}_{\leq 0}, defined by

F12​([a,b],[c],x)≔∑k≥0(a)k​(b)k(c)k​k!​xk,{}_{2}F_{1}([a,b],[c];x)\coloneqq\sum_{k\geq 0}\frac{(a)_{k}(b)_{k}}{(c)_{k}k!}x^{k}, (11)

where (a)k=a(a+1)⋯(a+k−1)(a)_{k}=a(a+1)\cdots(a+k-1) denotes the rising factorial. Indeed, p⁡(x)p(x) in Eq. 5 is equal to 2π⋅F12([−1/2,1/2],[1];x2)2\pi\cdot{}_{2}F_{1}([-1/2,1/2],[1];x^{2}), while ∫Cωx\int_{C}\omega_{x} in Eq. 10 is equal to 2​π⋅F12​([1/2,1/2],[1],x)2\pi\cdot{}_{2}F_{1}([1/2,1/2],[1];x). We have seen that in both cases these functions are transcendental.

In general, y⁡(x)=F12​([a,b],[c],x)y(x)={}_{2}F_{1}([a,b],[c];x) satisfies the second-order differential equation

x⁡(x−1)​y′′​(x)+((a+b+1)​x−c)​y′​(x)+a​b​y​(x)=0x(x-1)y^{\prime\prime}(x)+((a+b+1)x-c)y^{\prime}(x)+aby(x)=0 (12)

and the name hypergeometric comes from the fact that the coefficient sequence (uk)k≥0(u_{k})_{k\geq 0} of F12​([a,b],[c],x)=∑k≥0uk​xk{}_{2}F_{1}([a,b],[c];x)=\sum_{k\geq 0}u_{k}x^{k} satisfies a linear recurrence of order 1, namely

(a+k)​(b+k)​uk=(k+1)​(k+c)​uk+1,(k≥0).(a+k)(b+k)u_{k}=(k+1)(k+c)u_{k+1},\qquad(k\geq 0).

For other choices of parameters we recover the functions

(1−x)α\displaystyle(1-x)^{\alpha} =F12​([−α,1],[1],x),for all​α∈ℚ,\displaystyle={}_{2}F_{1}([-\alpha,1],[1];x),\quad\text{for all}\;\alpha\in\mathbb{Q},
∑k≥0Ck​xk\displaystyle\sum_{k\geq 0}C_{k}x^{k} =F12​([1,1/2],[2],4​x),\displaystyle={}_{2}F_{1}([1,1/2],[2];4x),
log⁡(1−x)\displaystyle\log(1-x) =−x⋅F12([1,1],[2];x),\displaystyle=-x\cdot{}_{2}F_{1}([1,1],[2];x),
arcsin⁡(x)\displaystyle\arcsin(x) =x⋅F12​([1/2,1/2],[3/2],x2),\displaystyle=x\cdot{}_{2}F_{1}([1/2,1/2],[3/2];x^{2}),

the first two of which are algebraic, the last two of which are transcendental. In some cases, the Gauss’ hypergeometric function even becomes a polynomial: this is so for

Pn​(x)=F12​([−n,n+1],[1],(1−x)/2),P_{n}(x)={}_{2}F_{1}([-n,n+1],[1];(1-x)/2),

the Legendre polynomial given by Pn​(x)≔12n⋅n!⋅∂n∂xn​(x2−1)nP_{n}(x)\coloneqq\frac{1}{2^{n}\cdot n!}\cdot\frac{\partial^{n}}{{\partial x}^{n}}(x^{2}-1)^{n}, as well as for

Tn​(x)=(−1)n⋅F12​([−n,n],[1/2],(x+1)/2),T_{n}(x)=(-1)^{n}\cdot{}_{2}F_{1}([-n,n],[1/2];(x+1)/2),

the Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind given by Tn​(cos⁡x)=cos⁡(n​x)T_{n}(\cos x)=\cos(nx).

Deciding the algebraicity of F12{}_{2}F_{1} hypergeometric functions is an old problem, solved by Schwarz [76] using geometric tools (Riemann mappings, Schwarzian derivatives and sphere tilings by spherical triangles) and by Landau [64, 65] and Errera [42] using arithmetic tools (Eisenstein’s criterion for algebraic power series, and Dirichlet’s theorem on prime numbers in arithmetic progressions). Both approaches are algorithmic: Schwarz’s criterion reduces the problem to a table look-up after some preprocessing on the parameters a,b,ca,b,c; the Landau-Errera criterion amounts to checking a finite number of inequalities.

More precisely, let us assume that none of aa, bb, c−ac-a and c−bc-b is an integer (equivalently, the operator H(a,b;c)≔x(1−x)∂x2+(c−(a+b+1)x)∂x−abH(a,b;c)\coloneqq x(1-x)\partial_{x}^{2}+(c-(a+b+1)x)\partial_{x}-ab is irreducible) and let DD be the common denominator of a,ba,b and cc. Then, the Landau-Errera criterion says that the following assertions are equivalent:

  1. 1.

    the hypergeometric function F12​([a,b],[c],x){}_{2}F_{1}([a,b],[c];x) is algebraic;

  2. 2.

    the operator H⁡(a,b,c)H(a,b;c) admits only algebraic solutions;

  3. 3.

    for every ℓ<D\ell<D coprime with DD, either {ℓ​a}<{ℓ​c}<{ℓ​b}\{\ell a\}<\{\ell c\}<\{\ell b\} or {ℓ​b}<{ℓ​c}<{ℓ​a}.\{\ell b\}<\{\ell c\}<\{\ell a\}. (Here {x}\{x\} denotes the fractional part x−⌊x⌋x-\lfloor x\rfloor of xx.)

The last condition is equivalent to the fact that, for every ℓ<D\ell<D coprime with DD, the two sets {e2​π​i​ℓ​a,e2​π​i​ℓ​b}\{e^{2\pi i\ell a},e^{2\pi i\ell b}\} and {e2​π​i​ℓ​c,1}\{e^{2\pi i\ell c},1\} are interlaced on the unit circle. This “interlacing condition” was first proved by Landau [64, 65] to be necessary for the algebraicity of F12​([a,b],[c],x){}_{2}F_{1}([a,b],[c];x) and then proved to also be sufficient by Errera [42]; see also Stridsberg’s intermediate contribution [82], which relates the conditions in Eisenstein’s criterion to the ones in the Landau-Errera condition. In §3.3 we will see that Theorem 3.23 provides an extension of the Landau-Errera “interlacing criterion” to the generalized hypergeometric function Fss+1{}_{s+1}F_{s} defined by

Fss+1​([a1,…,as+1],[b1,…,bs],x)=∑k≥0(a1)k⋯(as+1)k(b1)k⋯(bs)kk!​xk.{}_{s+1}F_{s}([a_{1},\ldots,a_{s+1}],[b_{1},\ldots,b_{s}];x)=\sum_{k\geq 0}\frac{(a_{1})_{k}\cdots(a_{s+1})_{k}}{(b_{1})_{k}\cdots(b_{s})_{k}k!}x^{k}. (13)

2.2 Examples from Algebra: Diagonals

As proved in Section 1, algebraic functions are D-finite. A larger, yet very important, class of D-finite functions is formed by the diagonals of rational functions. By definition, the diagonal of a multivariate power series

F=∑(i1,…,in)∈ℕnai1,…,in​x1i1​⋯​xnin∈ℚ⁡[[x1,…,xn]]F=\sum_{{(i_{1},\dots,i_{n})\in\mathbb{N}^{n}}}a_{i_{1},\dotsc,i_{n}}x_{1}^{i_{1}}\dotsm x_{n}^{i_{n}}\;\in\mathbb{Q}[[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]]

is the univariate power series

Diag⁡(F)=∑i∈ℕai,…,i​ti∈ℚ⁡[[t]].\operatorname{Diag}(F)=\sum_{i\in\mathbb{N}}a_{i,\dotsc,i}t^{i}\;\in\mathbb{Q}[[t]].
Example 2.1 (Dyck bridges).

Let BnB_{n} be the number of {↑,→}\{\uparrow,\rightarrow\}-walks in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} from (0,0)(0,0) to (n,n)(n,n) (i.e., there are exactly BnB_{n} ways of going from the origin to (n,n)(n,n) using only North and East steps, see §2.3 for a more general context) and let B⁡(t)B(t) be its generating function ∑n≥0Bn​tn\sum_{n\geq 0}B_{n}t^{n}. Then,

B⁡(t)=Diag⁡(11−x−y)=∑n≥0(2​nn)​tn.B(t)=\operatorname{Diag}\left(\frac{1}{1-x-y}\right)=\sum_{n\geq 0}\binom{2n}{n}t^{n}.

This is perhaps the simplest example of a diagonal. By the binomial theorem, it comes that B⁡(t)=1/1−4​tB(t)={1}/{\sqrt{1-4t}}, hence this diagonal is even an algebraic function. This is not an accident. Indeed, a century ago Pólya [73] proved that diagonals of bivariate rational functions are algebraic. (Later, Furstenberg [50] showed that the converse also holds true.) Pólya’s result can be proved as follows. First, using the simple observation11 1 Here, and in all the text, [xn][x^{n}] denotes coefficient extraction of xnx^{n}. Diag​(F)​(t)=[x0]​F​(x,t/x)\textsf{Diag}(F)(t)=[x^{0}]\,F(x,t/x), the diagonal of the rational function F⁡(x,y)∈ℚ⁡(x,y)F(x,y)\in\mathbb{Q}(x,y) is encoded as a complex integral using Cauchy’s integral theorem (for some ϵ>0\epsilon>0)

Diag⁡(F)​(t)=[x−1]​1x​F​(x,tx)=12​π​i​∮|x|=ϵF⁡(x,tx)​d​xx,\operatorname{Diag}\left(F\right)(t)=[x^{-1}]\frac{1}{x}F\left(x,\frac{t}{x}\right)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{|x|=\epsilon}F\left(x,\frac{t}{x}\right)\,\frac{dx}{x},

which in a second step can be evaluated using the residues theorem as a sum of residues (precisely: the residues of F⁡(x,t/x)/xF(x,t/x)/x at its “small poles”, having limit 0 at t=0t=0). Each of these residues are algebraic functions, and so is their sum Diag​(F)\textsf{Diag}(F).

Example 2.2 (Dyck bridges, continued).

The proof sketched above directly concludes that

Diag⁡(11−x−y)=12​π​i​∮|x|=ϵd​xx−x2−t=11−2​x|x=1−1−4​t2=11−4​t.\operatorname{Diag}\left(\frac{1}{1-x-y}\right)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{|x|=\epsilon}\frac{dx}{x-x^{2}-t}={\left.{\frac{1}{1-2x}}\right|_{x=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4t}}{2}}=}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-4t}}.
Example 2.3.

Interestingly, Pólya’s result becomes false for more than two variables. A simple example is provided by the rational function 1/(1−x−y−z)=∑i,j,k(i+j+k)!i!​j!​k!​xi​yj​zk1/(1-x-y-z)=\sum_{i,j,k}\frac{(i+j+k)!}{i!j!k!}x^{i}y^{j}z^{k}, whose diagonal is

Diag⁡(11−x−y−z)=∑n≥0(3​n)!n!3​tn.\operatorname{Diag}\left(\frac{1}{1-x-y-z}\right)=\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{(3n)!}{n!^{3}}t^{n}.

The transcendence of this function can be proved in various ways, for instance by using asymptotics: Stirling’s formula implies that (3​n)!n!3∼32​π​27nn\frac{(3n)!}{n!^{3}}\sim\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\pi}\,\frac{27^{n}}{n} and the presence of the factor n−1n^{-1} is incompatible with algebraicity by Corollary 1.4. Another proof is based on rewriting

Diag⁡(11−x−y−z)=F12​([13,23],[1],27​t),\operatorname{Diag}\left(\frac{1}{1-x-y-z}\right)={}_{2}F_{1}\left(\left[\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3}\right],\left[1\right];27t\right), (14)

and by using the Schwarz or the Landau-Errera criteria mentioned above.

The diagonal in Eq. 14 is hypergeometric, hence D-finite. In general, there is no reason that the diagonal of a multivariate rational function be hypergeometric. However, that all such diagonals are D-finite functions is a general fact. In fact, much more holds: a theorem by Lipshitz [66] states that if F⁡(x1,…,xn)F(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) is a multivariate D-finite function22 2 This means that FF satisfies a system of nn linear partial differential equations, the ii-th one being an ordinary linear differential equation with respect to ∂∂xi\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}} and with polynomial coefficients in x1,…,xnx_{1},\ldots,x_{n}., then Diag⁡(F)\operatorname{Diag}(F) is D-finite.

The particular case where FF is rational is already interesting and nontrivial to prove. In this case, the argument is the following. First, as in the bivariate case, if F=P/Q∈ℚ⁡(x1,…,xn)∩ℚ⁡[[x1,…,xn]]F=P/Q\in\mathbb{Q}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\cap\mathbb{Q}[[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]], then the residue theorem allows to write (for some ϵ>0\epsilon>0)

Diag⁡(F)​(t)=1(2​π​i)n−1​∮|x1|=⋯=|xn−1|=ϵF⁡(x1,…,xn−1,tx1⋯xn−1)​dx1⋯dxn−1x1⋯xn−1,\operatorname{Diag}(F)(t)=\frac{1}{(2\pi i)^{n-1}}\mathop{\text{\Large$\oint_{\text{\normalsize$\scriptstyle|x_{1}|=\cdots=|x_{n-1}|=\epsilon$}}$}}\nolimits F\left(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1},\frac{t}{x_{1}\cdots x_{n-1}}\right)\frac{dx_{1}\cdots dx_{n-1}}{x_{1}\cdots x_{n-1}},

so that Diag⁡(F)​(t)\operatorname{Diag}(F)(t) is the period function of a (family of) rational functions. Its D-finiteness is then a consequence of the finite-dimensionality over ℂ⁡(t)\mathbb{C}(t) of the de Rham cohomology for the complement of the variety in 𝔸ℂ⁡(t)n\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbb{C}(t)} defined by the equations Q⁡(x1,…,xn)=0Q(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=0 and x1⋯xn=tx_{1}\cdots x_{n}=t. (This finiteness proof usually relies on a geometric argument in the smooth case, and on Hironaka’s resolution of singularities in the general case.) In more down-to-earth terms this proof guarantees, in a non-effective way, that repeated differentiation under the integral sign eventually produces a finite sequence of rational integrands that admit a linear combination with coefficients in ℚ⁡(t)\mathbb{Q}(t) that becomes an exact differential.

If f⁡(t)f(t) is the diagonal of a rational function, then not only is f⁡(t)f(t) D-finite, but in addition f⁡(t)f(t) is globally bounded, that is, f⁡(t)f(t) has a nonzero radius of convergence in ℂ\mathbb{C} and β⋅f⁡(α⋅t)∈ℤ⁡[[t]]\beta\cdot f(\alpha\cdot t)\in\mathbb{Z}[[t]] for some α,β∈ℤ∖{0}\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}. (Note that this second property is equivalent to the existence of an N∈ℕ∖{0}N\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\} such that f⁡(N​t)−f⁡(0)∈ℤ⁡[[t]]f(Nt)-f(0)\in\mathbb{Z}[[t]], as in Proposition 1.6.) The following beautiful conjecture predicts that the converse is also true; it was formulated by Christol in the late 1980s, see e.g. [31] and [33, Conjecture 4]:

Conjecture 2.4 (Christol’s conjecture).

For f⁡(t)∈ℚ⁡[[t]]f(t)\in\mathbb{Q}[[t]], the following properties are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    f⁡(t)=Diag⁡(F)f(t)=\operatorname{Diag}(F) for some F∈ℚ⁡(x1,…,xn)∩ℚ⁡[[x1,…,xn]]F\in\mathbb{Q}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\cap\mathbb{Q}[[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]];

  2. (2)

    f∈ℚ⁡[[t]]f\in\mathbb{Q}[[t]] is D-finite and globally bounded.

Christol’s conjecture is far from being proved; the following explicit problem, also due to Christol [33, p. 51], is a very particular case of Conjecture 2.4 and it is still open as of today.

Question 2.5.

Is

f⁡(t)\displaystyle f(t) =F23​([19,49,59],[1,13],36​t)\displaystyle={}_{3}F_{2}\left(\left[\frac{1}{9},\frac{4}{9},\frac{5}{9}\right],\left[1,\frac{1}{3}\right];3^{6}\,t\right)
=1+60​t+20475​t2+9373650​t3+4881796920​t4+⋯\displaystyle=1+60\,t+20475\,t^{2}+9373650\,t^{3}+4881796920\,t^{4}+\cdots

the diagonal of a rational power series?

Therefore, even understanding diagonals which are hypergeometric functions is a very difficult problem; for some recent progress see [24].

Another natural and difficult question is whether a given diagonal of a rational function is algebraic or transcendental. This question is directly connected to the main aim of this article. One may wonder whether it is possible to detect transcendence of a given diagonal f⁡(t)=Diag⁡(F)f(t)=\operatorname{Diag}(F) by reducing it modulo a prime pp, and proving the transcendence of f⁡(t)modpf(t)\bmod p over 𝔽p​(t)\mathbb{F}_{p}(t). Unfortunately, this strategy is systematically doomed to failure: indeed, even if the diagonal f⁡(t)f(t) is transcendental, its reduction modulo pp is necessarily algebraic! This was proved by Furstenberg in [50, Theorem 1]. For instance, the transcendental diagonal in (14) is equal to

(1+t)−1/4\displaystyle(1+t)^{-1/4} mod5,\displaystyle\;\bmod 5,
(1+6t+6t2)−1/6\displaystyle(1+6t+6t^{2})^{-1/6} mod7,\displaystyle\;\bmod 7,
(1+6t+2t2+8t3)−1/10\displaystyle(1+6t+2t^{2}+8t^{3})^{-1/10} mod11.\displaystyle\;\bmod 11.

On the other hand, the Christol-André conjecture (Conjecture 1.12) implies that if f⁡(t)f(t) is the diagonal of a rational function, then f⁡(t)f(t) is algebraic if and only if the condition (3b) is fulfilled. The direct implication is true without the Christol-André conjecture; it relies on three nontrivial facts: (i) the minimal-order LDE for a diagonal has only regular singularities with rational exponents [32]; (ii) the classification of local solutions of Fuchsian linear differential equations [74, §19]; (iii) if f⁡(t)f(t) is algebraic, then its minimal-order LDE has only algebraic solutions [36, §2]. If the condition (3b) fails, then by (i) and (ii) at least one local solution g⁡(t)g(t) around t=0t=0 of the minimal-order LDE for f⁡(t)f(t) involves logarithms, hence g⁡(t)g(t) is transcendental; then (iii) implies that f⁡(t)f(t) must be transcendental as well.

For instance, the diagonal in (14) admits t(27t−1)∂t2+(54t−1)∂t+6t\left(27t-1\right)\partial_{t}^{2}+\left(54t-1\right)\partial_{t}+6 as minimal-order differential equation, with local basis

1+6​t+90​t2+⋯andlog⁡(t)+(6​log⁡(t)+15)​t+⋯.1+6t+90t^{2}+\cdots\quad\text{and}\quad\log\!\left(t\right)+\left(6\log\!\left(t\right)+15\right)t+\cdots.

Hence it is transcendental.

As a final remark, note that Theorem 1.1 in [87] implies that for any prime p≠3p\neq 3, the reduction modulo pp of the F23{}_{3}F_{2} (transcendental) function from Question 2.5 is algebraic (of degree at most p54p^{54}). Hence, even if this F23{}_{3}F_{2} function is not known to be a diagonal of a rational function, its reductions modulo pp are known to behave as reductions modulo pp of diagonals of rational functions.

2.3 Examples from Combinatorics: Walks in the Quarter Plane

In combinatorics, studying the nature of generating functions is of primary importance; for instance, algebraicity may reveal essential (but potentially hidden) recursive structures of the combinatorial classes under consideration. In particular, many examples have been studied over the past decades in lattice path combinatorics, a subfield of enumerative combinatorics. A plethora of interesting mathematical phenomena occur even when restricting to the walks with small steps in the quarter plane ℕ2\mathbb{N}^{2}. These are walks in the lattice ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}, confined to the cone ℝ+2{\mathbb{R}}_{+}^{2} that start at the origin (0,0)(0,0) and use steps in a model (or stepset) 𝒮\mathscr{S} which is a fixed subset of the set of nearest-neighbor steps {↙,←,↖,↑,↗,→,↘,↓}.\{{\swarrow,}\ {\leftarrow,}\ {\nwarrow,}\ {\uparrow,}\ {\nearrow,}\ {\rightarrow,}\ {\searrow,}\ {\downarrow}\}. The systematic study of small step walks in ℕ2\mathbb{N}^{2} has been initiated by Bousquet-Mélou and Mishna in their germinal article [27]. An earlier reference on the topic, in a probabilistic context, is the book [45]. The study of generating functions of walks with small steps in the quarter plane now spans several decades and dozens of articles. For instance, in [38] the differential-algebraic nature of these generating functions is completely elucidated using tools from differential Galois theory. A survey with many references can be found in the recent article [13].

Given a model 𝒮⊆{↙,←,↖,↑,↗,→,↘,↓}\mathscr{S}\subseteq\{{\swarrow,}\ {\leftarrow,}\ {\nwarrow,}\ {\uparrow,}\ {\nearrow,}\ {\rightarrow,}\ {\searrow,}\ {\downarrow}\}, we denote by qi,j,n\color[rgb]{0,0,0}q_{i,j,n} the number of 𝒮\mathscr{S}-walks of length nn ending at (i,j)(i,j). The full counting sequence (qi,j,n)(i,j,n)∈ℕ3(q_{i,j,n})_{(i,j,n)\in\mathbb{N}^{3}} admits several interesting specializations, for instance en≔q0,0,ne_{n}\coloneqq q_{0,0,n}, the number of 𝒮\mathscr{S}-walks of length nn returning to (0,0)(0,0) (“excursions”) and qn≔∑i,j≥0qi,j,nq_{n}\coloneqq\sum_{i,j\geq 0}q_{i,j,n}, the number of 𝒮\mathscr{S}-walks with prescribed length nn.

To these sequences one attaches various functions, namely the full generating function

Q𝒮​(x,y,t)=∑n=0∞(∑i,j=0∞qi,j,n​xi​yj)​tn∈ℚ⁡[x,y]​[[t]],Q_{\mathscr{S}}(x,y,t)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\biggl(\sum_{i,j=0}^{\infty}q_{i,j,n}x^{i}y^{j}\biggr)t^{n}\;\in{\mathbb{Q}}[x,y][[t]],\vskip-2.56064pt

and its corresponding univariate specializations Q𝒮​(0,0,t)=∑n≥0en​tnQ_{\mathscr{S}}(0,0,t)=\sum_{n\geq 0}e_{n}t^{n} (“excursions generating function”), Q𝒮​(1,1,t)=∑n≥0qn​tnQ_{\mathscr{S}}(1,1,t)=\sum_{n\geq 0}q_{n}t^{n} (“length generating function”), Q𝒮​(1,0,t)Q_{\mathscr{S}}(1,0,t) and Q𝒮​(0,1,t)\color[rgb]{0,0,0}Q_{\mathscr{S}}(0,1,t) (“boundary returns”) and [x0]​Q𝒮​(x,1/x,t)[x^{0}]\,Q_{\mathscr{S}}(x,1/x,t) (“diagonal returns”).

The general question in this setting is: given a model 𝒮\mathscr{S}, what can be said about the generating function Q𝒮​(x,y,t)Q_{\mathscr{S}}(x,y,t), and its specializations? In particular, is Q𝒮​(x,y,t)Q_{\mathscr{S}}(x,y,t) algebraic? Is it at least D-finite? Does Q𝒮​(x,y,t)Q_{\mathscr{S}}(x,y,t) (or at least some of its specializations) admit closed-form expressions?

The model 𝒮={↑,→}\mathscr{S}=\{\uparrow,\rightarrow\} in Example 2.1 (Dyck bridges) is one of the simplest possible models. In that case, the generating function Q𝒮​(x,y,t)Q_{\mathscr{S}}(x,y,t) is algebraic. This is actually a particular case of a classical result stating that whenever 𝒮\mathscr{S} is included in {↑,↗,→,↘,↓}\{\ {\uparrow,}\ {\nearrow,}\ {\rightarrow,}\ {\searrow,}\ {\downarrow}\} or in {←,↖,↑,↗,→}\{{\leftarrow,}\ {\nwarrow,}\ {\uparrow,}\ {\nearrow,}\ {\rightarrow}\}, that is, if the walks are essentially 1-dimensional, then Q𝒮​(x,y,t)Q_{\mathscr{S}}(x,y,t) is algebraic.

For this reason, most studies in the area focus on the truly 2-dimensional cases, that is on models 𝒮\mathscr{S} that contain both a step oriented towards the horizontal and the vertical axes (see Figure 1 in [13]). A full classification is now available, according to the algebro-differential properties of Q𝒮​(x,y,t)Q_{\mathscr{S}}(x,y,t), but here we restrict to two examples.

2.3.1 Trident walks

Up to some canonical reductions, there are exactly 2323 models of walks with small steps in the quarter plane whose full generating function Q⁡(x,y,t)Q(x,y,t) is D-finite (with respect to x,yx,y and tt). They are displayed in Figure 4 in [13].

One of these models is that of the “trident walks”, with 𝒮={↖,↑,↗,↓}\mathscr{S}=\{{\nwarrow,}\ {\uparrow,}\ {\nearrow,}\ {\downarrow}\}. This is entry 77 in [13, Fig. 4] and in [18, Table 6]. There exist 11 trident walk of length 00 (the empty walk), 22 trident walks of length 11 ({↑},{↗}\{\uparrow\},\{\nearrow\}) and 77 trident walks of length 22 ({↑−↑},{↑−↓},{↑−↗},{↗−↖},{↗−↑},{↗−↗},{↗−↓}\{\uparrow-\uparrow\},\{\uparrow-\downarrow\},\{\uparrow-\nearrow\},\{\nearrow-\nwarrow\},\{\nearrow-\uparrow\},\{\nearrow-\nearrow\},\{\nearrow-\downarrow\}). The length generating function Q⁡(t)Q(t) is completely and uniquely defined by L5L_{5} and by the first coefficients [tk]​Q​(t)[t^{k}]Q(t) for k=0,…,14k=0,\ldots,14. The question is: how to determine the algebraic or transcendental nature of Q⁡(t)Q(t)?

Note that the asymptotic estimate qn∼γ​βn​nrq_{n}\sim\gamma\beta^{n}n^{r} in [13, Fig. 4], with γ=4/(3​π)\gamma=4/(3\sqrt{\pi}), β=4\beta=4, r=−1/2r=-1/2, is compatible with algebraicity, since r∈ℚ∖ℤ<0r\in\mathbb{Q}\setminus\mathbb{Z}_{<0}, β∈ℚ¯\beta\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}} and γ​Γ​(r+1)=4/3∈ℚ¯\gamma\Gamma(r+1)=4/3\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}. Hence we cannot conclude the transcendence using asymptotic arguments as in Example 2.3.

An interesting feature is that L5L_{5} admits a factorization L2⋅L1,a⋅L1,b⋅L1,cL_{2}\cdot L_{1,a}\cdot L_{1,b}\cdot L_{1,c}, where the three operators L1,⋆L_{1,\star} have order 1, and L2L_{2} has order 22. This type of factorization 2/1/⋯/12/1/\cdots/1 actually holds in all the cases 1–19 in [13, Fig. 4]. On the other hand, the algorithmic method (a variant of the creative telescoping mentioned in Section 2.1.1) that produces the differential equation L5L_{5} does not guarantee that it is the least-order one satisfied by Q⁡(t)Q(t). In [18], the above factorization was algorithmically computed and exploited (together with some other computer algebra algorithms) in order to produce the following expression for Q⁡(t)Q(t) (and similar expressions for all cases 1–19 in [13, Fig. 4]):

From such an expression, it is not difficult to prove that Q⁡(t)Q(t) is transcendental, using the fact that the F12{}_{2}F_{1} occurring in the complete elliptic integral of the first kind, F12​([1/2,1/2],[1],t){}_{2}F_{1}([1/2,1/2],[1];t), is transcendental. In [18, §4.2] it was shown that Q⁡(t)Q(t) is transcendental by exploiting the explicit factorization of L5L_{5}, and by applying to L2L_{2} a specific algorithm that decides algebraicity of solutions for operators of order 2, namely Kovacic’s algorithm [62]. The same approach uniformly works on the models 1–19 and allows to prove the transcendence of the corresponding Q⁡(t)Q(t) except in case 17 for the model 𝒮={↑,←,↘}\mathscr{S}=\{\uparrow,\leftarrow,\searrow\} and in case 18 for the model 𝒮={↑,←,↘,↓,→,↖}\mathscr{S}=\{\uparrow,\leftarrow,\searrow,\downarrow,\rightarrow,\nwarrow\} (in these two cases the algorithm proves algebraicity of all solutions of the corresponding L2L_{2}). Very interestingly, the full generating function Q⁡(x,y,t)Q(x,y,t) is proved to be transcendental in all cases 1–19, and cases 17 and 18 are the only ones with algebraic specialization Q⁡(1,1,t)Q(1,1,t).

An alternative proof of the transcendence of the length generating function Q⁡(t)Q(t) for trident walks is based on the fact that L5L_{5} is indeed the minimal-order differential equation for Q⁡(t)Q(t); this implies that if Q⁡(t)Q(t) were algebraic, then L5L_{5} would only have algebraic solutions, a situation discarded by exhibiting logarithms in the local solutions of L5L_{5} at t=0t=0. This approach to the proof of transcendence of solutions of linear differential equations is used in [22]; its heart is the “minimization” algorithm from [21].

2.3.2 Gessel walks

The most difficult model of small-step walks in the quarter plane is Gessel’s model, for which 𝒮={↗,↙,←,→}\mathscr{S}={\{\nearrow,\swarrow,\leftarrow,\rightarrow\}}. For notational simplicity we will write G⁡(x,y,t)G(x,y,t) for the full generating function in this case, and G⁡(t)G(t) for the length generating function for Gessel walks G⁡(1,1,t)G(1,1,t).

Around 2000, Ira Gessel formulated two conjectures equivalent to the following statements:

Conjecture 2.6.

The generating function G⁡(0,0,t)=1+2​t2+11​t4+85​t6+782​t7+⋯G(0,0,t)=1+2t^{2}+11t^{4}+85t^{6}+782t^{7}+\cdots of Gessel excursions is equal to F23​([5/6,1/2,1],[5/3,2],16​t2).{{}_{3}F_{2}}\left([5/6,1/2,1],[5/3,2];16t^{2}\right).

Conjecture 2.7.

The generating function G⁡(x,y,t)G(x,y,t) is not D-finite.

Gessel’s first conjecture was first solved in 2009 by Kauers, Koutschan and Zeilberger in [58] using a computerized guess-and-prove approach. Unfortunately, solving Conjecture 2.6 had no implication concerning Conjecture 2.7, and in particular on the D-finiteness of the length generating function G⁡(t)G(t). It came as a total surprise when Bostan and Kauers [19] proved that Gessel’s second conjecture was false.

Theorem 2.8 ([19]).

The generating function G⁡(x,y,t)G(x,y,t) for Gessel walks is algebraic.

Moreover, the coefficients (gn)(g_{n}) of G⁡(t)=1+2​t+7​t2+21​t3+78​t4+260​t5+⋯G(t)=1+2t+7t^{2}+21t^{3}+78t^{4}+260t^{5}+\cdots satisfy (3​n+1)​g2​n=(12​n+2)​g2​n−1(3n+1)\,g_{2n}=(12n+2)\,g_{2n-1} and (n+1)​g2​n+1=(4​n+2)​g2​n(n+1)\,g_{2n+1}=(4n+2)\,g_{2n} for all n≥0n\geq 0.

In addition, G⁡(t)=(H⁡(t)−1)/(2​t)G(t)=(H(t)-1)/(2t) where H⁡(t)=1+2​t+4​t2+14​t3+42​t4+⋯H(t)=1+2t+4t^{2}+14t^{3}+42t^{4}+\cdots is a root of 27​(4​t−1)2​H​(t)8−18​(4​t−1)2​H​(t)4−8​(16​t2+24​t+1)​H​(t)2−(4​t−1)2=027\left(4t-1\right)^{2}H(t)^{8}-18\left(4t-1\right)^{2}H(t)^{4}-8\left(16t^{2}+24t+1\right)H(t)^{2}-\left(4t-1\right)^{2}=0, and

H⁡(t)=F12​([−112,14],[23],−64​t​(4​t+1)2(4​t−1)4).H(t)={{}_{2}{{}{{F_{1}}}}\!\left(\left[-\frac{1}{12},\frac{1}{4}\right],\left[\frac{2}{3}\right];-\frac{64t\left(4t+1\right)^{2}}{\left(4t-1\right)^{4}}\right)}.

The original discovery and proof of Theorem 2.8 was computer-driven, and used a guess-and-prove approach, based on Hermite-Padé approximants. As a byproduct of this proof, the minimal polynomial of G⁡(x,y,t)G(x,y,t) has been estimated to have more than 101110^{11} terms when written in expanded form, for a total size of ≈30\approx 30 Gb (!). The guess-and-prove method is a 3-step process: (i) compute G⁡(x,y,t)G(x,y,t) to precision t1200t^{1200} (≈1.5\approx 1.5 billion coefficients!); (ii) conjecture polynomial equations for G⁡(x,0,t)G(x,0,t) and G⁡(0,y,t)G(0,y,t); (iii) conclude the proof by computing multivariate resultants of (very big) polynomials (30 pages each).

As a matter of fact, the discovery of algebraicity was initially performed in a different way: the expansion of the generating function G⁡(x,y,t)G(x,y,t) modulo t1000t^{1000} was sufficient to guess (by using differential Hermite-Padé approximants) two differential operators

  • •

    ℒx,0∈ℚ(x,t)⟨∂t⟩\mathscr{L}_{x,0}\in\mathbb{Q}(x,t)\langle\partial_{t}\rangle, of order 11 in ∂t\partial_{t}, bidegree (96,78)(96,78) in (t,x)(t,x), and integer coefficients of at most 61 digits

  • •

    ℒ0,y∈ℚ(y,t)⟨∂t⟩\mathscr{L}_{0,y}\in\mathbb{Q}(y,t)\langle\partial_{t}\rangle, of order 11 in ∂t\partial_{t}, bidegree (68,28)(68,28) in (t,y)(t,y), and integer coefficients of at most 51 digits

such that ℒx,0​(G⁡(x,0,t))=0modt1000\;\mathscr{L}_{x,0}({G(x,0,t)})=0\bmod t^{1000} and ℒ0,y​(G⁡(0,y,t))=0modt1000\mathscr{L}_{0,y}({G(0,y,t)})=0\bmod t^{1000}.

After this guessing step of plausible differential equations for Q⁡(x,0,t)Q(x,0,t) and for Q⁡(0,y,t)Q(0,y,t), an important step in the discovery process was to apply Conjecture 1.13 with several primes pp. More precisely, for randomly chosen prime numbers pp, and a,b∈𝔽pa,b\in\mathbb{F}_{p}, both ℒa,0\mathscr{L}_{a,0} and ℒ0,b\mathscr{L}_{0,b} right-divide the pure power ∂tp\partial_{t}^{p} in 𝔽p(x)⟨∂t⟩\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)\langle\partial_{t}\rangle; in other terms, they have zero pp-curvature for all the tested primes pp (see Definition 3.18). This was the key observation in the discovery [19] that the trivariate generating function for Gessel walks is algebraic.

Several human proofs of Conjecture 2.6 and Theorem 2.8 have been discovered since the publication of [19]: the first one used complex analysis [20], the second one is purely algebraic [26], the third one is both combinatorial and analytic [28], while the more recent one is probably the most elementary [8].

2.4 Examples from Number Theory

In his ICM 2018 paper [89, p. 768], Zagier introduced a recurrent sequence of rational numbers (cn)n≥0(c_{n})_{n\geq 0} defined by initial terms c0=1,c1=−161/(210⋅35)c_{0}=1,c_{1}=-161/(2^{10}\cdot 3^{5}) and c2=26605753/(223⋅312⋅52)c_{2}=26605753/(2^{23}\cdot 3^{12}\cdot 5^{2}), and by the following linear recursion with polynomial coefficients:

cn−3+20​(4500​n2−18900​n+19739)​cn−2+80352000​n​(5​n−1)​(5​n−2)​(5​n−4)​cn\displaystyle c_{n-3}+20\left(4500n^{2}-18900n+19739\right)c_{n-2}+80352000n(5n-1)(5n-2)(5n-4)c_{n}
+25​(2592000​n4−16588800​n3+39118320​n2−39189168​n+14092603)​cn−1=0.\displaystyle\hskip-28.45274pt+25\left(2592000n^{4}-16588800n^{3}+39118320n^{2}-39189168n+14092603\right)c_{n-1}=0.

This mysteriously looking sequences arises from a topological differential equation in the work of Bertola, Dubrovin and Yang [9], each coefficient cnc_{n} being defined by an integral over the Deligne-Mumford moduli spaces of stable curves of genus gg with nn marked points. It is not difficult to prove that cnc_{n} behaves asymptotically like 1/n!21/n!^{2}. Inspired by an analogy with the behavior of the quantum periods in mirror symmetry, Zagier asked whether it is possible that the cnc_{n}’s become integers after multiplication by n!2n!^{2}, or more generally by the product of two rising factorials. Zagier mentions the following highly nontrivial two results:

  • •

    [Yang & Zagier]: an≔(210⋅35⋅54)n⋅(3/5)n⋅(4/5)n⋅cn∈ℤa_{n}\coloneqq(2^{10}\cdot 3^{5}\cdot 5^{4})^{n}\cdot({\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}3/5})_{n}\cdot({\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}4/5})_{n}\cdot c_{n}\in\mathbb{Z} for all integers n≥0n\geq 0;

  • •

    [Dubrovin & Yang]: bn≔(212⋅35⋅54)n⋅(2/5)n⋅(9/10)n⋅cn∈ℤb_{n}\coloneqq(2^{12}\cdot 3^{5}\cdot 5^{4})^{n}\cdot({\color[rgb]{1,0,1}2/5})_{n}\cdot({\color[rgb]{1,0,1}9/10})_{n}\cdot c_{n}\in\mathbb{Z} for all integers n≥0n\geq 0.

Both sequences are integer sequences of exponential growth, and hence can be expected to have a generating series that is (the Taylor expansion at 00 of) a period function in the sense of algebraic geometry. For the sequence (bn)(b_{n}), Zagier mentions that its generating function is even algebraic, but that the sequence (an)(a_{n}) seems to be more challenging. Yurkevich [88, Theorem 2] proved that the generating function of the sequence (an)(a_{n}) is also algebraic. (See [40, Thm. 2] for a very closely related result.) Inspired by these results, it is natural to look at the following question.

Question 2.9.

Find (u,v)∈ℚ(u,v)\in\mathbb{Q} such that c~n≔wn⋅(u)n⋅(v)n⋅cn∈ℤ\widetilde{c}_{n}\coloneqq w^{n}\cdot(u)_{n}\cdot(v)_{n}\cdot c_{n}\in\mathbb{Z} for all n≥0n\geq 0, for some w∈ℤw\in\mathbb{Z}.

A heuristic check is based on Conjecture 1.13: it is not difficult to check (using a computer-algebra system) that the remainder of the right Euclidean division of ∂xp\partial_{x}^{p} by ℒ4\mathscr{L}_{4} is zero for all primes 5<p<1005<p<100 except for p∈{7,31}p\in\{7,31\}. Conjecture 1.13 then suggests that indeed ℒ4\mathscr{L}_{4} possesses algebraic solutions only.

3 Grothendieck’s conjecture

The examples presented in §2 motivate the following question: given the linear differential equation (1) with coefficients in ℚ⁡(x)\mathbb{Q}(x), can we give necessary and/or sufficient conditions for admitting algebraic solutions (either one, or all of them)?

As already mentioned earlier, Grothendieck’s conjecture (Conjecture 1.13) provides such a criterion: in its enhanced version (Conjecture 3.17) it relates the existence of a “full basis of algebraic solutions” of the differential equation (1) to the existence of a “full basis of rational solutions” of its reductions modulo almost all prime numbers pp.

The aim of this section is, first of all, to introduce the notion of pp-curvature and to state a precise version of Grothendieck’s conjecture. We first examine in detail the case of first order equations in §3.1 and come to the general case in §3.2. The next sections are more focussed on the pp-curvature itself: in §4, we describe efficient methods for computing it in practice, while in §5, we examine how it controls the growth of denominators and, in particular, the integrality of the solutions of the starting differential equation.

3.1 The case of equations of order 11

Consider a linear differential operator of order 11

ℒ=∂x+a(x)\mathscr{L}=\partial_{x}+a(x) (15)

with a⁡(x)∈ℚ⁡(x)a(x)\in\mathbb{Q}(x). It makes sense to consider the reduction a⁡(x)​mod​p∈𝔽p​(x)a(x)\,\text{\rm mod}\,p\in\mathbb{F}_{p}(x) of (the coefficients of) a⁡(x)a(x) modulo pp for almost all prime numbers pp. Thus, one can consider the reduction

ℒp=∂x+a(x)modp\mathscr{L}_{p}=\partial_{x}+a(x)\,\text{\rm mod}\,p (16)

of ℒ\mathscr{L} modulo pp for almost all primes pp. This is a linear differential operator of order 11 with coefficients in 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x). Our aim is to relate the existence of a nonzero algebraic solution of (15) to the existence of nonzero rational solutions of the reduced equations (16).

In what follows, we say that a function ff is a solution of ℒ\mathscr{L} (resp. of ℒp\mathscr{L}_{p}) when it is a solution of the corresponding differential equation, i.e. when ℒ⁡(f)=0\mathscr{L}(f)=0 (resp. ℒp​(f)=0\mathscr{L}_{p}(f)=0).

3.1.1 Rational and algebraic solutions in characteristic 00: a criterion

What makes the case of first order equations tractable is the fact that there is an explicit criterion for the existence of a nonzero algebraic (or rational) solution.

Proposition 3.1.

The monic first order differential operator (15) has a nonzero rational (resp. algebraic) solution if and only if its constant coefficient a⁡(x)a(x) has at most a simple pole with integral (resp. rational) residue at each point of ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}} and vanishes at ∞\infty.

Proof.

We first consider the “rational case”. Let us first assume that a⁡(x)a(x) has at most a simple pole with integral residue at each point of ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}} and vanishes at ∞\infty. We thus have

a⁡(x)=∑i=1mnix−aia(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{n_{i}}{x-a_{i}} (17)

for some ai∈ℚ¯a_{i}\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}} and some ni∈ℤn_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}. A straightforward calculation shows that

f⁡(x)=∏i=1m(x−ai)nif(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{m}(x-a_{i})^{n_{i}} (18)

is a nonzero rational solution of (15).

Conversely, assume that (15) has a nonzero rational solution f⁡(x)f(x). This f⁡(x)f(x) can be factored as a product of linear factors f⁡(x)=c​∏i=1m(x−ai)nif(x)=c\prod_{i=1}^{m}(x-a_{i})^{n_{i}} with c∈ℚ¯×c\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}^{\times}, ai∈ℚ¯a_{i}\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}} and ni∈ℤn_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}. A straightforward calculation yields

a⁡(x)=f′​(x)f⁡(x)=∑i=1mnix−ai.a(x)=\frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{f(x)}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{n_{i}}{x-a_{i}}.

This shows that a⁡(x)a(x) has at most a simple pole with integral residue at each point of ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}} and vanishes at ∞\infty, as expected.

We now consider the “algebraic case”. Let us first assume that a⁡(x)a(x) has at most a simple pole with rational residue at each point of ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}} and vanishes at ∞\infty. Then, we can argue as we did above in the rational case, the only differences being that the nin_{i} involved in (17) are no longer in ℤ\mathbb{Z} but in ℚ\mathbb{Q} and that (18) is no longer rational but algebraic.

Conversely, assume that (15) has a nonzero algebraic solution f⁡(x)f(x). Let M⁡(Y)=YN+∑i=0N−1mi​(x)​Yi∈ℚ⁡(x)​[Y]M(Y)=Y^{N}+\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}m_{i}(x)Y^{i}\in\mathbb{Q}(x)[Y] be the minimal polynomial of f⁡(x)f(x) over ℚ⁡(x)\mathbb{Q}(x). By differentiating the equality M⁡(f)=0M(f)=0 with respect to xx and by using f′​(x)=a⁡(x)​f​(x)f^{\prime}(x)=a(x)f(x), we get

0=M​(f)′=N​fN−1​f′+∑i=0N−1mi′​(x)​fi+∑i=0N−1mi​(x)​i​fi−1​f′=N​fN−1​a​(x)​f+∑i=0N−1mi′​(x)​fi+∑i=0N−1mi​(x)​i​fi−1​a​(x)​f=N​a​(x)​fN+∑i=0N−1(mi′​(x)+mi​(x)​i​a​(x))​fi.0=M(f)^{\prime}=Nf^{N-1}f^{\prime}+\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}m_{i}^{\prime}(x)f^{i}+\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}m_{i}(x)if^{i-1}f^{\prime}\\ =Nf^{N-1}a(x)f+\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}m_{i}^{\prime}(x)f^{i}+\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}m_{i}(x)if^{i-1}a(x)f\\ =Na(x)f^{N}+\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}(m_{i}^{\prime}(x)+m_{i}(x)ia(x))f^{i}.

Hence, the polynomial P⁡(Y)=N​a​(x)​YN+∑i=0N−1(mi′​(x)+mi​(x)​i​a​(x))​YiP(Y)=Na(x)Y^{N}+\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}(m_{i}^{\prime}(x)+m_{i}(x)ia(x))Y^{i} satisfies P⁡(f)=0P(f)=0. By minimality of M⁡(Y)M(Y), we get P⁡(Y)=N​a​(x)​M​(Y)P(Y)=Na(x)M(Y). Equating the constant terms in this equality, we get that m0​(x)m_{0}(x) is a nonzero solution in ℚ⁡(x)\mathbb{Q}(x) of y′​(x)=N​a​(x)​y​(x)y^{\prime}(x)=Na(x)y(x). Using the “rational case” treated above, we get that N​a​(x)Na(x) has at most a simple pole with integral residue at each point of ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}} and vanishes at ∞\infty. Hence, a⁡(x)a(x) has at most a simple pole with rational residue at each point of ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}} and vanishes at ∞\infty, as expected. ∎

Note that the proof above is very similar (in fact, generalizes) the one used in Example 1.2 to prove that the exponential function is transcendental.

3.1.2 Algebraic solutions: from characteristic 00 to characteristic pp

We shall now consider the following question: assuming that (15) has a nonzero algebraic solution, what can be said about the reduced equation (16)? It is natural to expect that the latter has a nonzero algebraic solution as well for almost all primes pp. Actually, something even better happens.

Example 3.2.

Consider the differential equation

y′=12​(x−1)​y.y^{\prime}=\frac{1}{2(x-1)}y. (19)

It has a nonzero algebraic solution, namely f⁡(x)=(1−x)1/2f(x)=(1-x)^{1/2}. For any prime p≠2p\neq 2, one can consider the reduction of (19) modulo pp. Any such reduced equation has a nonzero algebraic solution, namely fp​(x)=(1−x)1/2f_{p}(x)=(1-x)^{1/2}. Let us clarify our notations: fp​(x)f_{p}(x) is a root of the polynomial Y2−(1−x)∈𝔽p​(x)​[Y]Y^{2}-(1-x)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)[Y], whereas f⁡(x)f(x) is a root of the polynomial Y2−(1−x)∈ℚ⁡(x)​[Y]Y^{2}-(1-x)\in\mathbb{Q}(x)[Y]. However, the reduction of (19) modulo pp can also be written as y′=npx−1​yy^{\prime}=\frac{n_{p}}{x-1}y where np∈ℤn_{p}\in\mathbb{Z} is such that np≡12​mod​pn_{p}\equiv\frac{1}{2}\,\text{\rm mod}\,p and, hence f~p​(x)=(1−x)np\widetilde{f}_{p}(x)=(1-x)^{n_{p}} is a nonzero solution of the reduction modulo pp of (19). The interesting point is that f~p​(x)\widetilde{f}_{p}(x) is not only algebraic but rational, contrary to fp​(x)f_{p}(x)!

The conclusion of Example 3.2 is a general fact as shown by Theorem 3.5 below. Let us first give an analogue in positive characteristic of the “rational case” of Proposition 3.1.

Proposition 3.3.

Consider b​(x)∈𝔽p​(x)b(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}(x). The differential equation

y′+b⁡(x)​y=0y^{\prime}+b(x)y=0

has a nonzero rational solution if and only if b⁡(x)b(x) has at most a simple pole with residue in 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} at each point of 𝔽p¯\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}} and vanishes at ∞\infty.

Proof.

The proof is entirely similar to the proof of the rational case of Proposition 3.1, it is sufficient to replace everywhere ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}} by 𝔽p¯\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}} and ℤ\mathbb{Z} by 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}. ∎

Example 3.4.

Consider the differential equation

y′=1x2+1​yy^{\prime}=\frac{1}{x^{2}+1}y (20)

whose general solution in characteristic zero is c⋅exp⁡(arctan⁡(x))c\cdot\exp(\arctan(x)) where cc is a constant. We are interested in determining whether or not this equation has a rational solution in characteristic p>0p>0. Modulo p=2p=2, the rational function b⁡(x)=1/(x2+1)b(x)=1/(x^{2}+1) writes 1/(x+1)21/(x+1)^{2}; thus it has a pole of order 22 and hence the differential equation (20) has no nonzero rational solutions by Proposition 3.3. For p≠2p\neq 2, the partial fraction decomposition of b⁡(x)b(x) reads

b⁡(x)=i2⋅(1x+i−1x−i)b(x)=\frac{i}{2}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{x+i}-\frac{1}{x-i}\right)

where ii denotes a square root of −1-1 in 𝔽p¯\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}}. We now need to distinguish between two cases depending on the congruence class of pp modulo 44. Indeed, when p≡1(mod4)p\equiv 1\pmod{4}, we have i∈𝔽pi\in\mathbb{F}_{p} and so the residues belong to 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} as well. In this case, the equation (20) has then a nonzero rational solution, namely

y⁡(x)=(x+ix−i)i/2,y(x)=\left(\frac{x+i}{x-i}\right)^{i/2},

where the exponent i/2i/2 is a lift in ℤ\mathbb{Z} of i/2∈𝔽pi/2\in\mathbb{F}_{p}. On the contrary, when p≡3(mod4)p\equiv 3\pmod{4}, we know that −1-1 is not a square in 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}, showing that the residues are not in 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} either. Therefore, in this case, the equation (20) has no nonzero rational solution.

Theorem 3.5.

If (15) has a nonzero algebraic solution, then, for almost all primes pp, (16) has a nonzero rational solution.

Proof.

Proposition 3.1 (and its proof) ensures that

a⁡(x)=∑i=1meix−aia(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{e_{i}}{x-a_{i}} (21)

for some ai∈ℚ¯a_{i}\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}} and some ei∈ℚe_{i}\in\mathbb{Q}.

Let us first assume that the aia_{i}’s belong to ℚ\mathbb{Q}. For any prime pp, we let ℤ(p)\mathbb{Z}_{(p)} be the ring of rational numbers with denominator relatively prime to pp. We denote by πp:ℤ(p)→𝔽p\pi_{p}:\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{p} the “reduction modulo pp” map. For almost all primes pp, the aia_{i}’s and the eie_{i}’s belong to ℤ(p)\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}. For any such pp, we have:

a⁡(x)​mod​p=∑i=1mπp​(ei)x−πp​(ai)a(x)\,\text{\rm mod}\,p=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{\pi_{p}(e_{i})}{x-\pi_{p}(a_{i})}

and the result follows from Proposition 3.3.

The proof in the general case is similar but requires basic notions from algebraic number theory. Let KK be a number field containing the aia_{i} and the eie_{i}. Let 𝒪K\mathcal{O}_{K} be the ring of integers of KK. For any prime 𝔓\mathfrak{P} of KK (which is by definition a prime ideal of 𝒪K\mathcal{O}_{K}), we let 𝒪𝔓{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathfrak{P}} be the valuation ring of KK at 𝔓\mathfrak{P}. We denote by κ𝔓\kappa_{\mathfrak{P}} the corresponding residue field and by π𝔓:𝒪𝔓→κ𝔓\pi_{\mathfrak{P}}:{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathfrak{P}}\rightarrow\kappa_{\mathfrak{P}} the quotient map. The residue field κ𝔓\kappa_{\mathfrak{P}} is a finite field of characteristic pp such that 𝔓∩ℤ=(p)\mathfrak{P}\cap\mathbb{Z}=(p). We say that 𝔓\mathfrak{P} is above pp. For almost all primes pp, for all primes 𝔓\mathfrak{P} of KK above pp, the aia_{i}’s and the eie_{i}’s belong to 𝒪𝔓{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathfrak{P}}. For such pp and 𝔓\mathfrak{P}, we have:

a⁡(x)​mod​p=a⁡(x)​mod​𝔓=∑i=1mπ𝔓​(ei)x−π𝔓​(ai).a(x)\,\text{\rm mod}\,p=a(x)\,\text{\rm mod}\,\mathfrak{P}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{\pi_{\mathfrak{P}}(e_{i})}{x-\pi_{\mathfrak{P}}(a_{i})}.

Since eie_{i} is rational, π𝔓​(ei)\pi_{\mathfrak{P}}(e_{i}) belongs to the prime subfield 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} of κ𝔓\kappa_{\mathfrak{P}}. The result follows from Proposition 3.3. ∎

3.1.3 From characteristic pp to characteristic 00

It is now tempting to ask: if (16) has a nonzero rational solution for almost all primes pp, does (15) have a nonzero algebraic solution? The (positive) answer is given by the following result.
