Theorem 3.6 (Honda [53]).

The converse of Theorem 3.5 holds true, i.e., if, for almost all primes pp, (16) has a nonzero rational solution, then (15) has a nonzero algebraic solution.

Proof.

Consider the partial fraction decomposition of a⁡(x)a(x):

a⁡(x)=P⁡(x)+∑i=1m∑j=1riαi,j(x−ai)ja(x)=P(x)+\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{r_{i}}\frac{\alpha_{i,j}}{(x-a_{i})^{j}}

with P​(x)∈ℚ¯​[x]P(x)\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[x], ai∈ℚ¯a_{i}\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}, αi,j∈ℚ¯\alpha_{i,j}\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}} and rj∈ℤ≥1r_{j}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}. According to Proposition 3.1, we have to prove that P⁡(x)P(x) and the αi,j\alpha_{i,j}’s for j≥2j\geq 2 are 00 and that the αi,1\alpha_{i,1}’s belong to ℚ\mathbb{Q}.

Let KK be a number field containing the aia_{i}, the αi,j\alpha_{i,j}’s and the coefficients of P⁡(x)P(x). We will use the notation and terminology (prime 𝔓\mathfrak{P} of KK, valuation ring 𝒪𝔓{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathfrak{P}}, quotient map π𝔓\pi_{\mathfrak{P}}, etc.) introduced in the proof of Theorem 3.5. For almost all primes pp, for all primes 𝔓\mathfrak{P} of KK above pp, the aia_{i}’s, the αi,j\alpha_{i,j}’s and the coefficients of P⁡(x)P(x) belong to 𝒪𝔓{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathfrak{P}}. For such pp and 𝔓\mathfrak{P}, we have:

a⁡(x)​mod​p=a⁡(x)​mod​𝔓=Pπ𝔓​(x)+∑i=1m∑j=1riπ𝔓​(αi,j)(x−π𝔓​(ai))j,a(x)\,\text{\rm mod}\,p=a(x)\,\text{\rm mod}\,\mathfrak{P}=P^{\pi_{\mathfrak{P}}}(x)+\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{r_{i}}\frac{\pi_{\mathfrak{P}}(\alpha_{i,j})}{(x-\pi_{\mathfrak{P}}(a_{i}))^{j}},

where Pπ𝔓​(x)P^{\pi_{\mathfrak{P}}}(x) denotes the polynomial obtained from P⁡(x)P(x) by applying π𝔓\pi_{\mathfrak{P}} coefficientwise.

Proposition 3.3 ensures that, for almost all primes pp, a⁡(x)​mod​pa(x)\,\text{\rm mod}\,p has at most simple poles, so, for almost all primes pp, for all primes 𝔓\mathfrak{P} of KK above pp, for all j∈{2,…,ri}j\in\{2,\ldots,r_{i}\}, we have π𝔓​(αi,j)=0\pi_{\mathfrak{P}}(\alpha_{i,j})=0, i.e., αi,j∈𝔓\alpha_{i,j}\in\mathfrak{P}. This implies that, for all j∈{2,…,ri}j\in\{2,\ldots,r_{i}\}, we have αi,j=0\alpha_{i,j}=0. Similarly, Proposition 3.3 also ensures that, for almost all primes pp, a⁡(x)​mod​pa(x)\,\text{\rm mod}\,p vanishes at ∞\infty, so, for almost all primes pp, for all primes 𝔓\mathfrak{P} of KK above pp, Pπ𝔓​(x)=0P^{\pi_{\mathfrak{P}}}(x)=0. This implies that P⁡(x)=0P(x)=0. Last, Proposition 3.3 ensures that, for almost all primes pp, for all primes 𝔓\mathfrak{P} above pp, we have π𝔓​(αi,1)∈𝔽p\pi_{\mathfrak{P}}(\alpha_{i,1})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}. Using Kronecker’s Theorem recalled below, we get that αi,1\alpha_{i,1} belongs to ℚ\mathbb{Q} and Proposition 3.1 yields the desired result: (15) has a nonzero algebraic solution. ∎

The Kronecker Theorem mentioned above (which is usually seen as a consequence of Chebotarev’s density Theorem) reads as follows

Theorem 3.7 (Kronecker).

An irreducible element P⁡(x)P(x) of ℚ⁡[x]\mathbb{Q}[x] such that, for almost all primes pp, P⁡(x)​mod​pP(x)\,\text{\rm mod}\,p has a zero in 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} is linear.

3.1.4 Rational solutions in characteristic pp and pp-curvature

Consider a differential equation

y′+b⁡(x)​y=0y^{\prime}+b(x)y=0 (22)

with b​(x)∈𝔽p​(x)b(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}(x). We will give an alternative criterion (an alternative to Proposition 3.3) for determining whether (22) has a nonzero rational solution based on the notion of pp-curvature that we shall now introduce.

Consider the 𝔽p​(xp)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x^{p})-linear map

Δ:𝔽p​(x)\displaystyle\Delta:\mathbb{F}_{p}(x) →\displaystyle\rightarrow 𝔽p​(x)\displaystyle\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)
f\displaystyle f ↦\displaystyle\mapsto f′+b⁡(x)​f.\displaystyle f^{\prime}+b(x)f.

The additivity is clear, the homogeneity follows from the fact that the elements of 𝔽p​(xp)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x^{p}) are constants of (the differential field) 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x) in the sense that their derivative is 00 (more precisely, 𝔽p​(xp)={f⁡(x)∈𝔽p​(x)|f′​(x)=0}\mathbb{F}_{p}(x^{p})=\{f(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)\ |\ f^{\prime}(x)=0\}) implying that (α​f)′=α​f′(\alpha f)^{\prime}=\alpha f^{\prime} for all α∈𝔽p​(xp)\alpha\in\mathbb{F}_{p}(x^{p}) and f∈𝔽p​(x)f\in\mathbb{F}_{p}(x).

Definition 3.8.

The map

Δp:𝔽p​(x)→𝔽p​(x)\Delta^{p}:\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)

is called the pp-curvature of (22).

A remarkable and fundamental fact is that the pp-curvature is not only 𝔽p​(xp)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x^{p})-linear but it is also 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)-linear. Indeed, a simple induction along with the Leibniz rule show that, for all k≥0k\geq 0, for all α,f∈𝔽p​(x)\alpha,f\in\mathbb{F}_{p}(x), we have

Δk​(α​f)=∑i=0k(ki)​α(i)​Δk−i​(f).\Delta^{k}(\alpha f)=\sum_{i=0}^{k}\binom{k}{i}\alpha^{(i)}\Delta^{k-i}(f).

Taking k=pk=p and using the fact that (pi)≡0modp\binom{p}{i}\equiv 0\bmod p for all 1<i<p1<i<p, we get

Δp​(α​f)=α(p)+α​Δp​(f),\Delta^{p}(\alpha f)=\alpha^{(p)}+\alpha\Delta^{p}(f),

and therefore the 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)-homogeneity follows from the fact that α(p)=0\alpha^{(p)}=0.

Proposition 3.9.

The differential equation (22) has a nonzero rational solution if and only if Δp=0\Delta^{p}=0.

Proof.

If (22) has a nonzero rational solution ff, then Δ⁡(f)=0\Delta(f)=0 and, hence, Δp​(f)=0\Delta^{p}(f)=0. As Δp\Delta^{p} is 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)-linear, we get Δp=0\Delta^{p}=0. Conversely, if Δp=0\Delta^{p}=0, then Δ\Delta has a nonzero kernel and, hence, (22) has a nonzero rational solution. ∎

Remark 3.10.

An easy calculation shows that, if (22) has pp-curvature 00, then an explicit nonzero rational solution is given by

∑k=0p−1(−1)k​xkk!​Δk​(1).\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^{k}\frac{x^{k}}{k!}\Delta^{k}(1).

We conclude this section by giving inductive and closed formulae for the pp-curvature. As it is 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)-linear, the pp-curvature is entirely determined by its value at 11:

∀f∈𝔽p​(x),Δp​(f)=Δp​(1)​f.\forall f\in\mathbb{F}_{p}(x),\ \Delta^{p}(f)=\Delta^{p}(1)f.

For this reason, we often say that the pp-curvature of (22) is Δp​(1)\Delta^{p}(1). It turns out that the pp-curvature Δp​(1)\Delta^{p}(1) can be calculated inductively. Indeed, for all k≥0k\geq 0, we denote by bk​(x)∈𝔽p​(x)b_{k}(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}(x) the constant term of the differential operator (∂x+b(x))k\big(\partial_{x}+b(x)\big)^{k}, so that

(∂x+b(x))k=∂xk+⋆∂xk−1+⋯+⋆∂x+bk(x),\big(\partial_{x}+b(x)\big)^{k}=\partial_{x}^{k}+\star\partial_{x}^{k-1}+\cdots+\star\partial_{x}+b_{k}(x), (23)

where ⋆\star are some unspecified elements of 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x). Equating the terms of degree 00 (with respect to ∂x\partial_{x}) in the equality (∂x+b(x))k+1=(∂x+b(x))⋅(∂x+b(x))k(\partial_{x}+b(x))^{k+1}=(\partial_{x}+b(x))\cdot(\partial_{x}+b(x))^{k}, we get the following inductive formula for computing the bk​(x)b_{k}(x)’s:

∀k≥0,bk+1​(x)=bk′​(x)+b⁡(x)​bk​(x).\forall k\geq 0,\ b_{k+1}(x)=b_{k}^{\prime}(x)+b(x)b_{k}(x). (24)

This gives the expected inductive formula for the pp-curvature of (22), since this is equal to

Δp​(1)=bp​(x).\Delta^{p}(1)=b_{p}(x).
Remark 3.11.

When k=pk=p, it is actually possible to determine the coefficients ⋆\star in equation (23). Indeed, we observe that (∂x+b(x))p(\partial_{x}+b(x))^{p} is a central element in 𝔽p(x)⟨∂x⟩\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)\langle\partial_{x}\rangle. This shows that the right-hand side of equation (23) must be central as well, implying eventually that all terms in ∂xi\partial_{x}^{i} with 0≤i<p0\leq i<p have to vanish, and that bp​(x)b_{p}(x) belongs to 𝔽p​(xp)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x^{p}).

In conclusion, we have the relation

(∂x+b(x))p=∂xp+bp(x).\big(\partial_{x}+b(x)\big)^{p}=\partial_{x}^{p}+b_{p}(x).

From this, we deduce that bp​(x)b_{p}(x) is also the opposite of the remainder in the right Euclidean division of ∂xp\partial_{x}^{p} by ℒ=∂x+b(x)\mathscr{L}=\partial_{x}+b(x). In particular, the pp-curvature vanishes if and only if ℒ\mathscr{L} divides ∂xp\partial_{x}^{p} in 𝔽p(x)⟨∂x⟩\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)\langle\partial_{x}\rangle.

Last, one can deduce from (24) the following remarkable closed formula (that does not extend to higher order equations).

Theorem 3.12.

We have bp​(x)=b(p−1)​(x)+b​(x)pb_{p}(x)=b^{(p-1)}(x)+b(x)^{p}.

Proof (after Jacobson [54]).

For a positive integer kk, let IkI_{k} be the set of all tuples α¯=(α1,…,αk)\underline{\alpha}=(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}) of nonnegative integers such that ∑i=1ki​αi=k\sum_{i=1}^{k}i\alpha_{i}=k. A calculation shows that bk​(x)b_{k}(x) is explicitly given by

bk(x)=∑α¯∈Ikλα¯⋅b(x)α1⋅b(1)(x)α2⋯b(k−1)(x)αk,b_{k}(x)=\sum_{\underline{\alpha}\in I_{k}}\lambda_{\underline{\alpha}}\cdot b(x)^{\alpha_{1}}\cdot b^{(1)}(x)^{\alpha_{2}}\cdots b^{(k-1)}(x)^{\alpha_{k}},

where λα¯\lambda_{\underline{\alpha}} is a coefficient in ℤ\mathbb{Z} determined by the following rule

λα¯=∑i=1k(αi−1+1)⋅λτi​(α¯)(for ​α¯∈Ik​),\lambda_{\underline{\alpha}}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}(\alpha_{i-1}+1)\cdot\lambda_{\tau_{i}(\underline{\alpha})}\qquad\text{(for }\underline{\alpha}\in I_{k}\text{)},

where τi\tau_{i} denotes the function from IkI_{k} to Ik−1I_{k-1} defined by

τi​(α¯)=(α1,…,αi−2,αi−1−1,αi+1,αi+1,…,αk−1)\tau_{i}(\underline{\alpha})=(\alpha_{1},\,\ldots,\,\alpha_{i-2},\,\alpha_{i-1}{-}1,\,\alpha_{i}{+}1,\,\alpha_{i+1},\,\ldots,\,\alpha_{k-1})

and where we agree that λβ¯=0\lambda_{\underline{\beta}}=0 if β¯\underline{\beta} has one negative coordinate. From this relation, one can check by induction on kk that λα¯\lambda_{\underline{\alpha}} (with α¯=(α1,…,αk)∈Ik\underline{\alpha}=(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k})\in I_{k}) is given by the closed formula:

λα¯=k!(α1)!⋯(αk)!⋅(2!)α2⋅(3!)α3⋯(k!)αk.\lambda_{\underline{\alpha}}=\frac{k!}{(\alpha_{1})!\cdots(\alpha_{k})!\cdot(2!)^{\alpha_{2}}\cdot(3!)^{\alpha_{3}}\cdots(k!)^{\alpha_{k}}}.

In particular, when k=pk=p, we find that the λα¯\lambda_{\underline{\alpha}}’s vanish modulo pp for all α¯∈Ip\underline{\alpha}\in I_{p} (thanks to the numerator p!p!) except when α¯=(p,0,…,0)\underline{\alpha}=(p,0,\ldots,0) or α¯=(0,…,0,1)\underline{\alpha}=(0,\ldots,0,1) (because, in those cases, the numerator cancels with a factor p!p! in the denominator). Besides, in both cases, one finds λα¯=1\lambda_{\underline{\alpha}}=1. This concludes the proof. ∎

Remark 3.13.

Remarkably, the explicit formula of Theorem 3.12 provides a second proof of Proposition 3.3. Indeed, consider a rational function b​(x)∈𝔽p​(x)b(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}(x) and write its partial fraction decomposition

b⁡(x)=P⁡(x)+∑i=1m∑j=1riβi,j(x−bi)jb(x)=P(x)+\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{r_{i}}\frac{\beta_{i,j}}{(x-b_{i})^{j}}

where P⁡(x)P(x) is a polynomial, the bib_{i}’s are pairwise distinct elements of 𝔽p¯\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}} and βi,j∈𝔽p¯\beta_{i,j}\in\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}} with βi,ri≠0\beta_{i,r_{i}}\neq 0. Each bib_{i} is a pole of b⁡(x)b(x) of multiplicity rir_{i} and residue βi,1\beta_{i,1}. Moreover, b⁡(x)b(x) has an extra pole at infinity when the degree of P⁡(x)P(x) is positive. A direct computation now gives:

bp​(x)=P(p−1)​(x)+P​(x)p−∑i=1m∑1≤j≤rij≡1​ mod ​pβi,j(x−bi)j+p−1+∑i=1m∑j=1riβi,jp(x−bi)p​jb_{p}(x)=P^{(p-1)}(x)+P(x)^{p}-\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq j\leq r_{i}\\ j\equiv 1\text{ mod }p\end{subarray}}\frac{\beta_{i,j}}{(x-b_{i})^{j+p-1}}+\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{r_{i}}\frac{\beta_{i,j}^{p}}{(x-b_{i})^{pj}}

and we see that the latter is zero if and only if P⁡(x)P(x) vanishes and, for all i∈{1,…,m}i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}, we have ri=1r_{i}=1 and βi,1p=βi,1\beta_{i,1}^{p}=\beta_{i,1}, i.e. βi,1∈𝔽p\beta_{i,1}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}. After Proposition 3.9, we then recover by different means the result of Proposition 3.3.

Example 3.14.

Applying the above recipe with the differential operator

ℒp=∂x−1x2+1\mathscr{L}_{p}=\partial_{x}-\frac{1}{x^{2}+1}

of Example 3.4, we find that its pp-curvature is explicitly given by

bp​(x)=−cp(x2+1)pb_{p}(x)=-\frac{c_{p}}{(x^{2}+1)^{p}}

where cp=1c_{p}=1 if p=2p=2, cp=0c_{p}=0 for p≡1(mod4)p\equiv 1\pmod{4} and cp=2c_{p}=2 for p≡3(mod4)p\equiv 3\pmod{4}. In particular, we retrieve by different means the dichotomy that we had already observed in Example 3.4.

The situation can be more complex if we slightly change the coefficient b⁡(x)b(x). For instance, consider the first-order differential operator:

ℒp=∂x−1x3−x−1.\mathscr{L}_{p}=\partial_{x}-\frac{1}{x^{3}-x-1}.

Its pp-curvature is zero if and only if the polynomial x3−x−1x^{3}-x-1 splits in 𝔽p​[x]\mathbb{F}_{p}[x] and p≠23p\neq 23. By [78, §5.3], this happens only for the primes p∈{59,101,167,173,211,223,271,307,317,…}p\in\{59,101,167,173,211,223,271,307,317,\ldots\} that have the property that p≠23p\neq 23 and they can be written as p=m2+m​n+6​n2p=m^{2}+mn+6n^{2} with m,n∈ℤm,n\in\mathbb{Z}, or equivalently, if and only if the coefficient of xp−1x^{p-1} in ∏n=1∞(1−xn)​(1−x23​n)\prod_{n=1}^{\infty}(1-x^{n})(1-x^{23n}) is equal to 2. (See also [84, Prop. 3.3].)

Remark 3.15.

There is a link between the pp-curvature of first-order linear differential operators and a fairly famous algorithm for factoring polynomials in 𝔽p​[x]\mathbb{F}_{p}[x], designed by Niederreiter in [68]. This connection seems to have been unnoticed until now. To factor a separable polynomial f=∏igif=\prod_{i}g_{i} of 𝔽p​[x]\mathbb{F}_{p}[x], with irreducible gig_{i}, Niederreiter considers the space of rational functions y=h/fy=h/f solutions of the equation y(p−1)+yp=0y^{(p-1)}+y^{p}=0, and shows that as a vector space over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} it is generated by the logarithmic derivatives gi′/gig_{i}^{\prime}/g_{i}. As a result, factoring boils down to a linear algebra problem over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}. This algorithm created a lot of excitement as a promising alternative to the much more classical one due to Berlekamp [7].

Putting together Theorem 3.5, Theorem 3.6, Proposition 3.9 and Remark 3.11, we obtain the following result.

Theorem 3.16.

Let ℒ=∂x+a(x)\mathscr{L}=\partial_{x}+a(x) as in equation (15) and, for almost all prime numbers pp, denote by ℒp\mathscr{L}_{p} its reduction modulo pp as in equation (16). The following properties are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    ℒ\mathscr{L} has a nonzero algebraic solution;

  2. (2)

    for almost all primes pp, ℒp\mathscr{L}_{p} has a nonzero rational solution;

  3. (3)

    for almost all primes pp, the pp-curvature of ℒp\mathscr{L}_{p} vanishes;

  4. (4)

    for almost all primes pp, the operator ℒp\mathscr{L}_{p} divides ∂xp\partial_{x}^{p} in 𝔽p(x)⟨∂x⟩\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)\langle\partial_{x}\rangle.

Grothendieck’s pp-curvature conjecture is a far reaching conjectural generalization of these equivalences for higher order equations.

3.2 The general case

Let us now consider a linear differential operator of arbitrary order:

ℒ=∂xn+an−1(x)⋅∂xn−1+⋯+a1(x)⋅∂x+a0(x)\mathscr{L}=\partial_{x}^{n}+a_{n-1}(x){\cdot}\partial_{x}^{n-1}+\cdots+a_{1}(x){\cdot}\partial_{x}+a_{0}(x) (25)

with ai​(x)∈ℚ​(x)a_{i}(x)\in\mathbb{Q}(x). As in the order-11 case, one can consider the reduction ℒp\mathscr{L}_{p} of ℒ\mathscr{L} modulo pp for almost all primes pp. This is a differential operator of order nn with coefficients in 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x). Grothendieck’s conjecture relates the algebraicity of the solutions of ℒ\mathscr{L} to the rationality of the solutions of ℒp\mathscr{L}_{p} for almost all primes pp.

First of all, we notice that the straightforward generalization of Theorem 3.16 cannot be true for higher order differential operators; indeed, we have seen in §2 many examples of differential equations that do not admit algebraic solutions and whose reductions modulo pp have nonzero rational solutions for almost all pp; this is the case, for instance, of most of hypergeometric functions and diagonals. The main new insight behind Grothendieck’s conjecture is the brilliant idea to replace the existence of a unique nonzero solution by the existence of a full basis of solutions.

We recall that the set of solutions of ℒ\mathscr{L} in ℚ⁡(x)¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}(x)} is a ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}}-vector space of dimension at most nn. When this dimension is maximal, that is, equal to nn, we say that ℒ\mathscr{L} has a full basis of algebraic solutions. Similarly, it is tempting to look at the set of solutions of ℒp\mathscr{L}_{p} in 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x) as an 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}-vector space. However, the example given by the differential equation y(p)=0y^{(p)}=0 shows that this vector space may be infinite dimensional (any element of 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x) is a solution of y(p)=0y^{(p)}=0). The point is that ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}} is the relevant base field in characteristic 00 because it is the field of differential constants of ℚ⁡(x)¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}(x)}. In characteristic pp, the field of differential constants of 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x) is not 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} but 𝔽p​(xp)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x^{p}); thus, a differential constant may depend on xx in characteristic pp (!) Now, one can prove that the set of solutions of ℒp\mathscr{L}_{p} in 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x) is an 𝔽p​(xp)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x^{p})-vector space of dimension at most nn. When this dimension is maximal, that is, equal to nn, we say that ℒp\mathscr{L}_{p} has a full basis of rational solutions.

We are now ready to state Grothendieck’s conjecture.

Conjecture 3.17 (Grothendieck’s conjecture).

For a differential operator ℒ∈ℚ(x)⟨∂x⟩\mathscr{L}\in\mathbb{Q}(x)\langle\partial_{x}\rangle as in equation (25), the following properties are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    ℒ\mathscr{L} has a full basis of algebraic solutions;

  2. (2)

    for almost all primes pp, ℒp\mathscr{L}_{p} has a full basis of rational solutions.

Consider the linear differential operator

ℒ=∂xn+bn−1(x)⋅∂xn−1+⋯+b1(x)⋅∂x+b0(x)\mathscr{L}=\partial_{x}^{n}+b_{n-1}(x){\cdot}\partial_{x}^{n-1}+\cdots+b_{1}(x){\cdot}\partial_{x}+b_{0}(x) (26)

with bi​(x)∈𝔽p​(x)b_{i}(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}(x). There is no straightforward generalization of Proposition 3.3 for determining whether (26) has a full basis of rational solutions but the criterion given by Proposition 3.9 via the pp-curvature does extend to higher order equations. Let us briefly explain this.

Let Y′+B⁡(x)​Y=0Y^{\prime}+B(x)Y=0 be the differential system associated to (26), where

B=(0−10⋯0000−1⋯00⋮⋮⋮⋮⋮⋮000⋯−10000⋯0−1b0b1b2⋯bn−2bn−1)∈Mn​(𝔽p​(x)).B=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccccc}0&-1&0&\cdots&0&0\\ 0&0&-1&\cdots&0&0\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\ 0&0&0&\cdots&-1&0\\ 0&0&0&\cdots&0&-1\\ b_{0}&b_{1}&b_{2}&\cdots&b_{n-2}&b_{n-1}\end{array}\right)\in M_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)). (27)

Mimicking what has been done in Section 3.1.4 in the order-11 case, we consider the 𝔽p​(xp)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x^{p})-linear map

Δ:𝔽p​(x)n\displaystyle\Delta:\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)^{n} →\displaystyle\rightarrow 𝔽p​(x)n\displaystyle\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)^{n}
F\displaystyle F ↦\displaystyle\mapsto F′+B⁡(x)​F.\displaystyle F^{\prime}+B(x)F.
Definition 3.18.

The map

Δp:𝔽p​(x)n→𝔽p​(x)n\Delta^{p}:\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)^{n}

is called the pp-curvature of (26).

As in the first-order case, one can easily prove that the pp-curvature is not only 𝔽p​(xp)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x^{p})-linear, but also 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)-linear. Moreover, the inductive formula (24) for computing the pp-curvature of equations of order 11 can be extended as follows: the matrix Bp​(x)B_{p}(x) of the pp-curvature with respect to the canonical basis is given by the recurrence

Bk+1​(x)=Bk′​(x)+B⁡(x)​Bk​(x)B_{k+1}(x)=B_{k}^{\prime}(x)+B(x)B_{k}(x) (28)

starting with B0​(x)=B​(x)B_{0}(x)=B(x).

The following fundamental result is a generalization of Proposition 3.9 to higher order differential equations. We recall the fact, already mentioned at the very beginning of Section 3.2, that the set of solutions of a given ℒ∈𝔽p(x)⟨∂x⟩\mathscr{L}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)\langle\partial_{x}\rangle in 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x) of order nn is an 𝔽p​(xp)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x^{p})-vector space of dimension at most nn and that, when this dimension is maximal, that is, equal to nn, we say that ℒ\mathscr{L} has a full basis of rational solutions.

Theorem 3.19 (Cartier’s lemma).

Let ℒ∈𝔽p(x)⟨∂x⟩\mathscr{L}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)\langle\partial_{x}\rangle be a differential operator as in equation (26). The following properties are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    ℒ\mathscr{L} has a full basis of rational solutions;

  2. (2)

    the pp-curvature of ℒ\mathscr{L} (that is Δp\Delta^{p}) vanishes;

  3. (3)

    ℒ\mathscr{L} divides ∂xp\partial_{x}^{p} in 𝔽p(x)⟨∂x⟩\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)\langle\partial_{x}\rangle.

Proof.

Let us first note that the following properties, relative to the 𝔽p​(xp)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x^{p})-vector space S≔ker⁡(Δ)S\coloneqq\ker(\Delta), are equivalent:

  1. i)

    the differential equation (26) has a full basis of rational solutions;

  2. ii)

    the 𝔽p​(xp)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x^{p})-vector space SS has dimension nn;

  3. iii)

    the 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)-vector space 𝔽p​(x)n\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)^{n} is spanned by SS.

The equivalence between i) and ii) follows immediately from the easily verifiable fact that the map

f⁡(x)↦(f⁡(x),f′​(x),…,f(n−1)​(x))f(x)\mapsto(f(x),f^{\prime}(x),\ldots,f^{(n-1)}(x))

induces an 𝔽p​(xp)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x^{p})-linear isomorphism from the 𝔽p​(xp)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x^{p})-vector space of solutions of ℒ\mathscr{L} in 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x) to the 𝔽p​(xp)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x^{p})-vector space SS. The equivalence between ii) and iii) follows from the “Wronskian lemma” [86, Lemma 1.12]. Indeed, the wronskian lemma ensures that any family of elements of SS is linearly dependent over 𝔽p​(xp)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x^{p}) if and only if it is linearly dependent over 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x). Therefore, the dimension of the 𝔽p​(xp)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x^{p})-vector space SS and the dimension of the 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)-vector space spanned by SS are equal. Considering the case where one or other of these dimensions is nn, we obtain the equivalence between ii) and iii).

We are now ready to prove the theorem.

Let us first prove (1)⟹\Longrightarrow(2). If ℒ\mathscr{L} has a full basis of rational solutions, then the implication i)⟹\Longrightarrowiii) ensures that the 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)-vector space 𝔽p​(x)n\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)^{n} is spanned by SS. Since Δp\Delta^{p} is 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)-linear and vanishes on SS, we have Δp=0\Delta^{p}=0.

Let us now prove (2)⟹\Longrightarrow(1). We assume that Δp=0\Delta^{p}=0. We claim that the 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)-vector space 𝔽p​(x)n\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)^{n} is spanned by SS. Consider the map

P:𝔽p​(x)n\displaystyle P:\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)^{n} →\displaystyle\rightarrow 𝔽p​(x)n\displaystyle\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)^{n}
F\displaystyle F ↦\displaystyle\mapsto ∑k=0p−1(−1)k​xkk!​Δk​(F).\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^{k}\frac{x^{k}}{k!}\Delta^{k}(F).

A simple calculation shows that

Δ⁡(P⁡(F))=−(−x)p−1​Δp​(F)=0\Delta(P(F))=-(-x)^{p-1}\Delta^{p}(F)=0

and, hence, PP has values in SS. But, another simple calculation shows that, for all F∈𝔽p​(x)nF\in\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)^{n}, we have

F=∑k=0p−1xkk!​P​(Δk​(F)).F=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{x^{k}}{k!}P(\Delta^{k}(F)).

This shows that the 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)-vector space 𝔽p​(x)n\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)^{n} is spanned by SS as claimed. Now, using the implication iii)⟹\Longrightarrowi), we get that ℒ\mathscr{L} has a full basis of rational solutions.

It remains to prove that (2)⟺\Longleftrightarrow(3). In order to do so, we first notice that, given rational functions f0​(x),…,fn−1​(x),g0​(x),…,gn−1​(x)f_{0}(x),\ldots,f_{n-1}(x),g_{0}(x),\ldots,g_{n-1}(x), the equality

Δ⁡(f0​(x),…,fn−1​(x))=(g0​(x),…,gn−1​(x))\Delta\big(f_{0}(x),\ldots,f_{n-1}(x)\big)=\big(g_{0}(x),\ldots,g_{n-1}(x)\big)

is equivalent to the following congruence in 𝔽p(x)⟨∂x⟩\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)\langle\partial_{x}\rangle:

(f0(x)+⋯+fn−1(x)∂xn−1)⋅∂x≡g0(x)+⋯+gn−1(x)∂xn−1(modℒ).\big(f_{0}(x)+\cdots+f_{n-1}(x)\partial_{x}^{n-1}\big)\cdot\partial_{x}\equiv g_{0}(x)+\cdots+g_{n-1}(x)\partial_{x}^{n-1}\pmod{\mathscr{L}}.

It follows from this observation that, writing Ei=(0,…,0,1,0,…,0)E_{i}=(0,\ldots,0,1,0,\ldots,0) with the coordinate 11 in ii-th position, the coordinates of Δp​(Ei)\Delta^{p}(E_{i}) are exactly the coefficients of the remainder in the division of ∂xp+i\partial_{x}^{p+i} by ℒ\mathscr{L}. Hence Δp​(Ei)\Delta^{p}(E_{i}) vanishes if and only if ℒ\mathscr{L} divides ∂xp+i\partial_{x}^{p+i}. The equivalence (2)⟺\Longleftrightarrow(3) follows immediately. ∎

Remark 3.20.

The three assertions of Theorem 3.19 are also equivalent to

  1. (4)

    ℒ\mathscr{L} admits nn power series solutions in 𝔽p​[[x]]\mathbb{F}_{p}[[x]], linearly independent over 𝔽p​((xp))\mathbb{F}_{p}((x^{p}));

  2. (5)

    ℒ\mathscr{L} admits nn polynomial solutions in 𝔽p​[x]\mathbb{F}_{p}[x], linearly independent over 𝔽p​((xp))\mathbb{F}_{p}((x^{p})).

The implication (4) ⟹\Longrightarrow (5) is proved in [53, Lemma 1], while (5) ⟹\Longrightarrow (1) and (1) ⟹\Longrightarrow (4) are trivial. Moreover, under the equivalent assertions (1)–(5), Proposition 1 in [23] shows that there exists a full basis of polynomial solutions in 𝔽p​[x]\mathbb{F}_{p}[x], each of them having degree less than p​dpd, where dd is the maximal degree of the numerators/denominators of the coefficients bi​(x)b_{i}(x) of ℒ\mathscr{L} in (26).

Remark 3.21.

Assume that ℒ\mathscr{L} has pp-curvature zero. An easy calculation shows that

U0​(x)=∑k=0p−1(−1)k​xkk!​Bk​(x)∈Mn​(𝔽p​(x))U_{0}(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^{k}\frac{x^{k}}{k!}B_{k}(x)\in M_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p}(x))

is a solution of Y′+B⁡(x)​Y=0Y^{\prime}+B(x)Y=0. If, moreover, B⁡(x)B(x) has no pole at 00, then U0​(x)U_{0}(x) has no pole at 00 as well and we have U0​(0)=InU_{0}(0)=I_{n}, so U0​(x)U_{0}(x) is a fundamental matrix of rational solutions of Y′+B⁡(x)​Y=0Y^{\prime}+B(x)Y=0. If B⁡(x)B(x) has a pole at 00, then U0​(x)U_{0}(x) is not necessarily invertible. Note that, more generally, if a∈𝔽pa\in\mathbb{F}_{p} is not a pole of B⁡(x)B(x), then

Ua​(x)=∑k=0p−1(−1)k​(x−a)kk!​Bk​(x−a)U_{a}(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^{k}\frac{(x-a)^{k}}{k!}B_{k}(x-a)

is a fundamental matrix of rational solutions of Y′+B⁡(x)​Y=0Y^{\prime}+B(x)Y=0.

Putting together all that precedes, we obtain a simple algorithm to determine whether (26) has a full basis of rational solutions: compute inductively Bp​(x)B_{p}(x) and, then, check whether Bp​(x)B_{p}(x) vanishes. Note however that no extension of the simple formula of Theorem 3.12 is known for higher order differential equations. Roughly speaking, this is due to the fact that, contrarily to 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x), the ring of n×nn\times n matrices over 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x) is noncommutative as soon as n≥2n\geq 2. Computing the pp-curvature is then much more complicated in this case but rather efficient algorithms for this task are nevertheless available; we will discuss them in Section 4.

Using Theorem 3.19 (Cartier’s lemma), we get the following reformulation of Grothendieck’s conjecture.

Conjecture 3.22 (Grothendieck’s conjecture in terms of pp-curvature).

For a differential operator ℒ\mathscr{L} as in equation (25), the following properties are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    ℒ\mathscr{L} has a full basis of algebraic solutions;

  2. (2)

    for almost all primes pp, the pp-curvature of ℒp\mathscr{L}_{p} vanishes;

  3. (3)

    for almost all primes pp, ℒp\mathscr{L}_{p} divides ∂xp\partial_{x}^{p} in the ring of differential operators 𝔽p(x)⟨∂x⟩\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)\langle\partial_{x}\rangle.

3.3 Progresses toward Grothendieck’s conjecture

3.3.1 A known case: the generalized hypergeometric equations

It is in general very difficult to determine whether a given differential equation has a full basis of algebraic solutions. In their celebrated work [10], Beukers and Heckman managed to do this for an important class of differential equations, omnipresent in the mathematical and physical literature, namely the generalized hypergeometric equations. In fact, Beukers and Heckman extended the Landau-Errera criterion mentioned in §2.1.3. Let 𝐚=(a1,…,as+1){\bf a}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{s+1}) and 𝐛=(b1,…,bs,bs+1=1){\bf b}=(b_{1},\ldots,b_{s},b_{s+1}=1) be two (s+1)(s+1)-tuples of rational parameters, assumed disjoint modulo ℤ\mathbb{Z}. This assumption is equivalent to the irreducibility in ℚ(x)⟨∂⟩\mathbb{Q}(x)\langle\partial\rangle of the “generalized hypergeometric operator” defined by

ℋ𝓎𝓅(𝐚,𝐛)≔(x∂x+b1−1)⋯(x∂x+bs−1)x∂x−x(x∂x+a1)⋯(x∂x+as+1).\mathscr{Hyp}({\bf a},{\bf b})\coloneqq(x\partial_{x}+b_{1}-1)\cdots(x\partial_{x}+b_{s}-1)x\partial_{x}-x(x\partial_{x}+a_{1})\cdots(x\partial_{x}+a_{s+1}).

It is easy to check that ℋ​𝓎​𝓅​(𝐚,𝐛)\mathscr{Hyp}({\bf a},{\bf b}) admits in its solution space the generalized hypergeometric function Fss+1​([a1,…,as+1],[b1,…,bs],x){}_{s+1}F_{s}([a_{1},\ldots,a_{s+1}],[b_{1},\ldots,b_{s}];x) defined in (13). The Beukers-Heckman result then reads as follows.

Theorem 3.23 (“interlacing criterion”, Beukers-Heckman, [10]).

Given two (s+1)(s+1)-tuples of rational numbers 𝐚=(a1,…,as+1){\bf a}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{s+1}) and 𝐛=(b1,…,bs,bs+1=1){\bf b}=(b_{1},\ldots,b_{s},b_{s+1}=1), assumed to be disjoint modulo ℤ\mathbb{Z}, let DD be the common denominator of their elements. Then, the following assertions are equivalent:

  1. 1.

    the hypergeometric function Fss+1​([a1,…,as+1],[b1,…,bs],x){}_{s+1}F_{s}([a_{1},\ldots,a_{s+1}],[b_{1},\ldots,b_{s}];x) is algebraic;

  2. 2.

    the operator ℋ​𝓎​𝓅​(𝐚,𝐛)\mathscr{Hyp}({\bf a},{\bf b}) admits a full basis of algebraic solutions;

  3. 3.

    for all 1≤ℓ<D1\leq\ell<D with gcd⁡(ℓ,D)=1\gcd(\ell,D)=1 the (s+1)(s+1)-tuples (e2​π​i​ℓ​aj)1≤j≤s+1(e^{2\pi i\ell a_{j}})_{1\leq j\leq s+1} and (e2​π​i​ℓ​bj)1≤j≤s+1(e^{2\pi i\ell b_{j}})_{1\leq j\leq s+1} interlace on the unit circle.

The interlacing condition mentioned in the latter result is defined as follows. We say that two (s+1)(s+1)-tuples (uj)1≤j≤s+1(u_{j})_{1\leq j\leq s+1} and (vj)1≤j≤s+1(v_{j})_{1\leq j\leq s+1} of elements of the unit circle interlace if, up to renumbering the uju_{j} and the vjv_{j}, we have u1=e2​π​i​α1,…,us+1=e2​π​i​αs+1u_{1}=e^{2\pi i\alpha_{1}},\ldots,u_{s+1}=e^{2\pi i\alpha_{s+1}} and v1=e2​π​i​β1,…,vs+1=e2​π​i​βs+1v_{1}=e^{2\pi i\beta_{1}},\ldots,v_{s+1}=e^{2\pi i\beta_{s+1}} with either

0≤α1<β1<α2<β2≤⋯<αs+1<βs+1<10\leq\alpha_{1}<\beta_{1}<\alpha_{2}<\beta_{2}\leq\cdots<\alpha_{s+1}<\beta_{s+1}<1

or

0≤β1<α1<β2<α2≤⋯<βs+1<αs+1<1.0\leq\beta_{1}<\alpha_{1}<\beta_{2}<\alpha_{2}\leq\cdots<\beta_{s+1}<\alpha_{s+1}<1.
Example 3.24.

The Beukers-Heckman criterion immediately implies that the operator ℋ​𝓎​𝓅​(𝐚,𝐛)\mathscr{Hyp}({\bf a},{\bf b}) admits a full basis of algebraic solutions for the choice

𝐚={130,730,1130,1330,1730,1930,2330,2930},𝐛={15,13,25,12,35,23,45,1}.{\bf a}=\left\{\frac{1}{30},\frac{7}{30},\frac{11}{30},\frac{13}{30},\frac{17}{30},\frac{19}{30},\frac{23}{30},\frac{29}{30}\right\},\quad{\bf b}=\left\{\frac{1}{5},\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{5},\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{5},\frac{2}{3},\frac{4}{5},1\right\}.

This proves in particular a beautiful observation due to Fernando Rodriguez-Villegas, namely that the generating function ∑n≥0un​xn\sum_{n\geq 0}u_{n}x^{n} of the sequence

un≔(30​n)!​n!(15​n)!​(10​n)!​(6​n)!u_{n}\coloneqq\frac{(30n)!n!}{(15n)!(10n)!(6n)!}

(used by Chebyshev in his work on estimates for the prime counting function) is algebraic.

Note that without the irreducibility assumption on ℋ​𝓎​𝓅​(𝐚,𝐛)\mathscr{Hyp}({\bf a},{\bf b}), the situation is much more subtle. For instance, F12​([1/2,1/3],[3/2],x){}_{2}F_{1}([1/2,1/3],[3/2];x) is transcendental, while F12​([3/2,1/3],[1/2],x){}_{2}F_{1}([3/2,1/3],[1/2];x) is algebraic. In a recent work by Fürnsinn and Yurkevich [52], a generalization of Theorem 3.23 is given, which allows to decide algebraicity/transcendence of arbitrary generalized hypergeometric functions (with potentially irrational parameters).

In addition to Theorem 3.23, Beukers and Heckman also drew up in [10] the list of generalized hypergeometric equations having a full basis of algebraic solutions, thus extending Schwarz’s classification of algebraic F12{}_{2}F_{1}’s [76].

On the other hand, a calculation due to Katz in [57, §5.5] (also in [55, §6] for the specific case of F12{}_{2}F_{1}’s) shows that this list coincides with the list of generalized hypergeometric equations whose reductions modulo pp have a full basis of rational solutions for almost all primes pp, in accordance with Grothendieck’s conjecture.

3.3.2 State of the art on Grothendieck’s conjecture

Besides for order-11 equations and for generalized hypergeometric equations, Grothendieck’s conjecture has been proved in several particular cases.

On the one hand, for Picard-Fuchs differential equations (satisfied by periods of a family of smooth algebraic varieties), and more generally for certain direct factors, Grothendieck’s conjecture was established by Katz [55]. As an application, Katz gave in [57, Theorem 5.5.3] a new proof of the aforementioned results of Beukers and Heckman [10] about the generalized hypergeometric equations. Katz [55, §1], and later André [5, §III], related the pp-curvatures to the reduction modulo pp of the Kodaira-Spencer map. (See also Foucault [48] and Foucault and Toffin [49] for explicit computations for families of curves of genus 2 and 3.) As explained in [5, p. 108], this approach has a potential of delivering effective versions of Grothendieck’s conjecture, similar to effective versions of Chebotarev’s density theorem [63, 77]: the hope is to obtain, for instance for any Picard-Fuchs operator ℒ\mathscr{L}, an integer N⁡(ℒ)N(\mathscr{L}) such that the fact that ℒ\mathscr{L} has a full basis of algebraic solutions can be read on the pp-curvatures of ℒ\mathscr{L} for the primes p<N⁡(ℒ)p<N(\mathscr{L}).

On the other hand, an arithmetic approach to Grothendieck’s conjecture was introduced by the Chudnovsky brothers [35] who proved Grothendieck’s conjecture for any rank one linear homogeneous differential equation over an algebraic curve [35, Theorem 8.1] (the case of first order equations over ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} had been proved by Honda in [53, §1], see Theorem 3.6). They also proved Grothendieck’s conjecture for the class of Lamé equations [35, Theorem 7.2], of the form

p⁡(x)​y′′​(x)+12​p′​(x)​y′​(x)−(n⁡(n+1)​x+B)⋅y⁡(x)=0p(x)y^{\prime\prime}(x)+\frac{1}{2}p^{\prime}(x)y^{\prime}(x)-\big(n(n+1)x+B\big){\cdot}y(x)=0

where n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, B∈ℚB\in\mathbb{Q} and p⁡(x)∈ℚ⁡[x]p(x)\in\mathbb{Q}[x] has degree 3. The arithmetic approach was extended by André to the case when the differential Galois group has a solvable neutral component [5] (see also [3], [4, Chap. VIII], [12, Thm. 2.9] and [29, Thm. 3.5]).

Katz [56] proposed a conjectural description of the differential Galois group in terms of pp-curvatures and he proved that his conjecture is equivalent to the initial conjecture by Grothendieck.

Using the language of schemes and sheaves, Grothendieck’s conjecture can be formulated more generally for differential equations over any algebraic smooth curve defined over a number field. In [5, Remark 7.1.4], André noticed that, using Belyi maps, one can reduce the general case to that of the curve X=ℙ1\{0,1,∞}X=\mathbb{P}^{1}\backslash\{0,1,\infty\}. In our setting, this means that one can safely assume that the differential operator ℒ\mathscr{L} has only singularities at 00, 11 and ∞\infty. Under this additional assumption, Tang [83] proves that if all33 3 When ℒ\mathscr{L} does not reduce properly at a prime pp, the pp-curvature of ℒp\mathscr{L}_{p} is a priori not defined; however Tang manages to give an alternative definition of the vanishing of the pp-curvature, see [83, Definition 2.1.7]. the pp-curvatures of ℒ\mathscr{L} vanish, then ℒ\mathscr{L} has a full basis of rational solutions. Although this latter result differs from Grothendieck’s in the hypotheses (which are stronger) and the conclusion (which is also stronger), it is closely related.

We also point out the work of Bost in [12] giving an algebraicity criterion for leaves of algebraic foliations defined over number fields. For additional details, we refer to [29]. We mention the work of van der Put in [85] concerned with inhomogeneous equations of order 11. Other special cases of the conjecture have been proven recently, see [44, 79, 71]. Last but not least, an analogue of Grothendieck’s conjecture for qq-difference equations was conjectured by Bézivin [11, §5] and proved by Di Vizio in [37].

3.4 A formal parallel with Kronecker’s theorem

It is instructive to observe that Grothendieck’s conjecture appears to be, in some sense, a differential version of Kronecker’s theorem we have already encountered earlier (see Theorem 3.7). Indeed, Kronecker’s theorem can be reformulated as follows.

Theorem 3.25.

For a separable polynomial L∈ℚ⁡[x]L\in\mathbb{Q}[x], the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    all the roots of LL are in ℚ\mathbb{Q};

  2. (2)

    for almost all primes pp, all the roots of L​ mod ​pL\text{ mod }p are in 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p};

  3. (3)

    for almost all primes pp, we have Xp≡X(modL,p)X^{p}\equiv X\pmod{L,p}.

It is striking that the three conditions of Theorem 3.25 are formal analogues of the conditions of Conjecture 3.17, at least if we admit that algebraic solutions in the differential case correspond to rational solutions in the algebraic case. Besides, the fact that the condition Xp≡X(modL,p)X^{p}\equiv X\pmod{L,p} translates to ∂xp≡0(modℒ,p)\partial_{x}^{p}\equiv 0\pmod{\mathscr{L},p}, i.e. that the right-hand side shifts from XX to 00, is explained by the fact that the classical Frobenius map behaves “multiplicatively” (it belongs naturally to some Galois group) while the pp-curvature behaves “additively” (it belongs naturally to some Lie algebra).

In the classical setting, Kronecker’s theorem is obtained as a corollary of Chebotarev’s density theorem, which is itself proved by means of Artin’s LL-functions. Unfortunately, similar tools do not seem to be available so far in the differential context; developing them might then sound as an exciting project.

As mentioned above, Honda proved that the Grothendieck conjecture for first order differential equations is equivalent to Kronecker’s theorem. In [35, §4], the Chudnovsky brothers gave an elementary (although “extravagant”) proof of these equivalent statements; their approach is based on Hermite’s explicit Hermite-Padé approximants to binomial functions. More precisely, they proved that if y′​(x)=xα​y​(x)y^{\prime}(x)=\frac{x}{\alpha}y(x) has zero pp-curvature for almost all primes pp, then for all primes ideals 𝔓\mathfrak{P} of ℚ⁡(α)\mathbb{Q}(\alpha) all the binomial coefficients (αn)\binom{\alpha}{n} are 𝔓\mathfrak{P}-integral for all nn. From there, it is shown that Hermite-Padé approximants to 1,xα,…,x(m−1)​α1,x^{\alpha},\ldots,x^{(m-1)\alpha} at x=1x=1 with weights (N,…,N)(N,\ldots,N) are trivial for large mm and NN. This in turn implies that 1,xα,…,x(m−1)​α1,x^{\alpha},\ldots,x^{(m-1)\alpha} are linearly dependent over ℚ⁡(x)\mathbb{Q}(x), that is xαx^{\alpha} is an algebraic function, which is equivalent to α∈ℚ\alpha\in\mathbb{Q}.

4 About the computation of the pp-curvature

After Cartier’s lemma (Theorem 3.19) and Grothendieck’s conjecture (Conjecture 3.17), it is clear that the pp-curvature is an invariant of primary importance of linear differential equations in characteristic pp. In this section, we outline some algorithms for computing it (or other quantities associated to it) efficiently.

4.1 Operators of order 11

In the case of differential equations of order 11 of the form (22):

y′+b⁡(x)​y=0y^{\prime}+b(x)y=0

we have seen in Theorem 3.12 that the pp-curvature is explicitly given by the formula

bp​(x)=b(p−1)​(x)+b​(x)p.b_{p}(x)=b^{(p-1)}(x)+b(x)^{p}.

Furthermore, computing explicitly the latter is quite an easy task which directly reduces to writing down the partial fraction decomposition of b⁡(x)b(x). Indeed, we have seen that if b⁡(x)b(x) decomposes as

b⁡(x)=P⁡(x)+∑i=1m∑j=1riαi,j(x−ai)jb(x)=P(x)+\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{r_{i}}\frac{\alpha_{i,j}}{(x-a_{i})^{j}}

then

bp​(x)=P(p−1)​(x)+P​(x)p−∑i=1m∑1≤j≤rij≡1​ mod ​pαi,j(x−ai)j+p−1+∑i=1m∑j=1riαi,jp(x−ai)p​j.b_{p}(x)=P^{(p-1)}(x)+P(x)^{p}-\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq j\leq r_{i}\\ j\equiv 1\text{ mod }p\end{subarray}}\frac{\alpha_{i,j}}{(x-a_{i})^{j+p-1}}+\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{r_{i}}\frac{\alpha_{i,j}^{p}}{(x-a_{i})^{pj}}.

Importantly for algorithmic purposes, we observe that the size of bp​(x)b_{p}(x) is roughly the same as the size of the input b⁡(x)b(x), although the degree of (the numerator and the denominator of) the former is pp times larger the degree of the latter. This apparent contradiction is explained by the fact that bp​(x)b_{p}(x) is actually a function of xpx^{p}; it is then a sparse rational function, in the sense that a large proportion of its coefficients vanish.

Remark 4.1.

Another option for computing explicitly the pp-curvature of differential operators of order 11 is presented in [23, Thm. 2]; it avoids the computation of partial fraction decomposition and the factorization of the denominator of b⁡(x)b(x). Let us briefly sketch it with the differential operator

∂x−1x2+1\partial_{x}-\frac{1}{x^{2}+1}

of Example 3.4. We write b(x)=−1/(x2+1)b(x)=-1/(x^{2}+1) and assume p>2p>2 for simplicity. In order to compute bp​(x)b_{p}(x), we expand b⁡(x)b(x) in power series:

b(x)=−∑n=0∞(−1)nx2​n.b(x)=-\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{n}x^{2n}.

The (p−1)(p{-}1)-st derivative of x2​nx^{2n} is 00 when 2​n≢−1(modp)2n\not\equiv-1\pmod{p}, and it is −x2​n−p+2-x^{2n-p+2} otherwise thanks to Wilson’s theorem. Writing 2​n=p−1+p​k2n=p-1+pk and noticing that kk has to be even, k=2​ℓk=2\ell, we end up with

b(p−1)(x)=−∑ℓ=0∞(−1)ℓ−p−12x2​ℓ​pb^{(p-1)}(x)=-\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{\ell-\frac{p-1}{2}}x^{2\ell p}

On the other hand, it is clear that b(x)p=−∑n=0∞(−1)nx2​n​p.b(x)^{p}=-\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{n}x^{2np}. Adding both sums, we find

bp(x)=−∑n=0∞(−1)n⋅(1−(−1)p−12)⋅x2​n​p.b_{p}(x)=-\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{n}\cdot\left(1-(-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}}\right)\cdot x^{2np}.

When p≡1(mod4)p\equiv 1\pmod{4}, the exponent p−12\frac{p-1}{2} is even and the term in the parenthesis vanishes. Therefore bp​(x)=0b_{p}(x)=0 in this case. On the contrary, when p≡3(mod4)p\equiv 3\pmod{4}, we have

bp(x)=−2⋅∑n=0∞(−1)n⋅x2​n​p=−21+x2​p=−2(1+x2)p.b_{p}(x)=-2\cdot\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{n}\cdot x^{2np}=-\frac{2}{1+x^{2p}}=-\frac{2}{(1+x^{2})^{p}}.

and we recover the result of Example 3.14.

The same idea applies actually to any differential operator ℒ=∂x−b(x)\mathscr{L}=\partial_{x}-b(x). Indeed, as already noticed its pp-curvature is a rational function in xpx^{p}. Besides, it is of the form f⁡(xp)/denom​(b⁡(x))pf(x^{p})/\text{denom}(b(x))^{p}, where f⁡(x)f(x) is a polynomial of degree at most d=deg⁡(b⁡(x))d=\deg(b(x)). Hence, it is enough to determine the power series expansion of (b​(x)(p−1))1/p(b(x)^{(p-1)})^{1/p} at precision xdx^{d}, starting from the power series expansion of b⁡(x)b(x) at the same precision dd. If b⁡(x)=∑n≥0un​xnb(x)=\sum_{n\geq 0}u_{n}x^{n}, then by Wilson’s theorem we have (b(x)(p−1))1/p=−∑n≥1un​p−1xn−1(b(x)^{(p-1)})^{1/p}=-\sum_{n\geq 1}u_{np-1}x^{n-1}, and hence it is enough to be able to compute the terms up−1,…,ud​p−1u_{p-1},\ldots,u_{dp-1}. Since b⁡(x)b(x) is a rational function, the sequence (un)n≥0(u_{n})_{n\geq 0} satisfies a linear recursion of order at most dd, with coefficients in 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} (given by the coefficients of denom​(b)\text{denom}(b)). As the NN-th term of such a linear recurrence with constant coefficients can be computed using O⁡(d​log⁡(d)​log​(N))O(d\log(d)\log(N)) operations in 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} using the technique of binary powering combined with fast polynomial multiplication in 𝔽p​[x]\mathbb{F}_{p}[x], we conclude that the pp-curvature bp​(x)b_{p}(x) can be computed by an algorithm that uses O⁡(d2​log⁡(d)​log⁡(p))O(d^{2}\log(d)\log(p)) operations in 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}.

Note that the reasoning above shows that the pp-curvature bp​(x)b_{p}(x) of ℒ=∂x−b(x)\mathscr{L}=\partial_{x}-b(x) is zero if and only if the following infinite systems of congruences holds

un≡u(n+1)​p−1(modp)for all​n≥0.u_{n}\equiv u_{(n+1)p-1}\pmod{p}\quad\text{for all}\;n\geq 0.

4.2 Reading the pp-curvature on the solutions

For differential equations of higher orders, the sparsity of the pp-curvature no longer holds in general. However, we have the following result.

Proposition 4.2.

Let

ℒ=∂xn+bn−1(x)⋅∂xn−1+⋯+b1(x)⋅∂x+b0(x)\mathscr{L}=\partial_{x}^{n}+b_{n-1}(x){\cdot}\partial_{x}^{n-1}+\cdots+b_{1}(x){\cdot}\partial_{x}+b_{0}(x)

with bi​(x)∈𝔽p​(x)b_{i}(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}(x) and let B⁡(x)B(x) be the associated companion matrix (see equation (27)). Let f​(x)∈𝔽p​[x]f(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[x] be a common denominator of the bi​(x)b_{i}(x)’s and

d=max⁡(deg⁡f⁡(x),deg⁡(f⁡(x)​b0​(x)),…,deg⁡(f⁡(x)​bn−1​(x))).d=\max\big(\deg f(x),\,\deg(f(x)b_{0}(x)),\,\ldots,\,\deg(f(x)b_{n-1}(x))\big).

Let Bp​(x)B_{p}(x) be the matrix of the pp-curvature of ℒ\mathscr{L} defined by the recurrence (28). Then, the following holds.

  • (i)

    The matrix Bp​(x)B_{p}(x) has the form 1f​(x)p​Cp​(x)\frac{1}{f(x)^{p}}C_{p}(x) where the entries of Cp​(x)C_{p}(x) are all polynomials of degree at most d​pdp.

  • (ii)

    The matrix Bp​(x)B_{p}(x) is similar to a matrix with coefficients in 𝔽p​(xp)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x^{p}).

The first assertion of the proposition follows easily from the induction formula (28) (see [23, Lemma 1]). The assertion (ii) is more subtle and requires the construction of a differential extension of 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x) over which ℒ\mathscr{L} has a full basis of solutions. We refer to [41, Proposition 2.1.2] for a detailed proof.

Besides, we notice that (ii) implies that the trace, the determinant of Bp​(x)B_{p}(x) and, more generally, all the coefficients of its characteristic polynomial lie in 𝔽p​(xp)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x^{p}). This latter statement can be also seen as a consequence of the following easy lemma: the determinant of a linear mapping 𝔽p​(x)n→𝔽p​(x)n\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)^{n}\to\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)^{n} commuting with ∇:F↦F′+B⁡(x)​F\nabla:F\mapsto F^{\prime}+B(x)F has zero derivative. This alternative proof has the advantage to avoid going to an extension. We derive from what precedes that the sizes of the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of Bp​(x)B_{p}(x) are comparable to the sizes of the bi​(x)b_{i}(x)’s, although the size of the pp-curvature itself is in general pp times larger.

In order to design fast algorithms for computing the pp-curvature, it is useful to go beyond Cartier’s lemma (see Theorem 3.19) and relate the pp-curvature to the shape of solutions. Let

ℒ=∂xn+bn−1(x)⋅∂xn−1+⋯+b1(x)⋅∂x+b0(x)\mathscr{L}=\partial_{x}^{n}+b_{n-1}(x){\cdot}\partial_{x}^{n-1}+\cdots+b_{1}(x){\cdot}\partial_{x}+b_{0}(x)

be a differential operator as before. In §3.2, we have seen that, when the pp-curvature of ℒ\mathscr{L} vanishes and the bi​(x)b_{i}(x)’s have no pole at 00, a fundamental system of solutions of ℒ\mathscr{L} is explicitly given by

∑k=0p−1(−1)k​Bk​(x)​xkk!\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^{k}B_{k}(x)\frac{x^{k}}{k!}

where the Bk​(x)B_{k}(x)’s are the matrices defined by the recurrence (28). In full generality, i.e. without assuming the vanishing of BpB_{p}, the idea is to consider the formal expansion

∑k=0∞(−1)k​Bk​(x)​xkk!.\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{k}B_{k}(x)\frac{x^{k}}{k!}.

Of course, this does not make sense in 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x) because of the division by k!k!, but we shall see that it does make sense in a suitable ring. A natural idea to achieve this goal is to introduce divided powers, i.e. to consider the ring of Hurwitz series, denoted by 𝔽p​[[x]]dp\mathbb{F}_{p}[[x]]^{\text{\rm dp}}, whose elements are formal series of the form

a0+a1​γ1​(x)+a2​γ2​(x)+⋯+ak​γk​(x)+⋯.a_{0}+a_{1}\gamma_{1}(x)+a_{2}\gamma_{2}(x)+\cdots+a_{k}\gamma_{k}(x)+\cdots.

In the above expression, the γk​(x)\gamma_{k}(x)’s are formal names without further additional meaning. Of course, they should be thought of as xkk!\frac{x^{k}}{k!} but we cannot write this division because the denominator may vanish. The multiplication on 𝔽p​[[x]]dp\mathbb{F}_{p}[[x]]^{\text{\rm dp}} is governed by the rule

γm​(x)⋅γn​(x)=(m+nm)⋅γn+m​(x)\gamma_{m}(x)\cdot\gamma_{n}(x)=\binom{m+n}{m}\cdot\gamma_{n+m}(x)

for any nonnegative integers mm and nn. Besides 𝔽p​[[x]]dp\mathbb{F}_{p}[[x]]^{\text{\rm dp}} is equipped with a natural derivation that takes ∑kak​γk​(x)\sum_{k}a_{k}\gamma_{k}(x) to ∑kak+1​γk​(x)\sum_{k}a_{k+1}\gamma_{k}(x). We have to be careful however that 𝔽p​[[x]]dp\mathbb{F}_{p}[[x]]^{\text{\rm dp}} is not a domain (e.g. γ1​(x)p=0\gamma_{1}(x)^{p}=0) and, because of that, we cannot consider its ring of fractions. But still, if the matrix B⁡(x)B(x) has polynomial coefficients, all the Bk​(x)B_{k}(x)’s have the same property and we can consider their images Bkdp​(x)B_{k}^{\text{\rm dp}}(x) is the ring Mn​(𝔽p​[[x]]dp)M_{n}\big(\mathbb{F}_{p}[[x]]^{\text{\rm dp}}\big). We then can form

Sdp​(x)=∑k=0∞(−1)k​Bkdp​(x)⋅γk​(x)S^{\text{\rm dp}}(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{k}B_{k}^{\text{\rm dp}}(x)\cdot\gamma_{k}(x) (29)

obtaining this way a fundamental matrix of solutions of ℒ\mathscr{L} over 𝔽p​[[x]]dp\mathbb{F}_{p}[[x]]^{\text{\rm dp}}. This construction works actually more generally as soon as the entries of B⁡(x)B(x) have no pole at zero: in this case, we can expand them as series in xx in order to view them in 𝔽p​[[x]]dp\mathbb{F}_{p}[[x]]^{\text{\rm dp}}. The precise relation between Sdp​(x)S^{\text{\rm dp}}(x) and the pp-curvature is given by the next lemma.

Lemma 4.3 (Bostan–Caruso–Schost [15]).

We have the matrix relation:

dp​Sdp​(x)d​xp=−Bpdp(x)⋅Sdp(x).\frac{d^{p}S^{\text{\rm dp}}(x)}{dx^{p}}=-B_{p}^{\text{\rm dp}}(x)\cdot S^{\text{\rm dp}}(x).
Proof.

Set M=𝔽p​[x]M=\mathbb{F}_{p}[x] and let Δ:Mn→Mn,Y↦d​Yd​x+B⁡(x)​Y.\Delta:M^{n}\to M^{n},Y\mapsto\frac{dY}{dx}+B(x)Y. By definition of the pp-curvature, Δp\Delta^{p} is the multiplication by Bp​(x)B_{p}(x).

Now consider the endomorphism Δdp\Delta^{\text{\rm dp}} of Mdp=𝔽p​[[x]]dp⊗𝔽p​[x]MM^{\text{\rm dp}}=\mathbb{F}_{p}[[x]]^{\text{\rm dp}}\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_{p}[x]}M defined by

Δdp=dd​x⊗idM+1⊗ΔM.\Delta^{\text{\rm dp}}=\frac{d}{dx}\otimes\text{\rm id}_{M}+1\otimes\Delta_{M}.

One checks that it satisfies the Leibniz rule: for f∈𝔽p​[[x]]dpf\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[[x]]^{\text{\rm dp}} and m∈Mm\in M, we have

Δdp​(f⊗m)=d​fd​x⊗m+f⊗Δ⁡(m).\Delta^{\text{\rm dp}}(f\otimes m)=\frac{df}{dx}\otimes m+f\otimes\Delta(m).

Hence, raising it to the pp-th power, we obtain

(Δdp)p​(Ydp)=dp​Ydpd​xp+Bpdp​(x)⋅Ydp(\Delta^{\text{\rm dp}})^{p}(Y^{\text{\rm dp}})=\frac{d^{p}Y^{\text{\rm dp}}}{dx^{p}}+B_{p}^{\text{\rm dp}}(x)\cdot Y^{\text{\rm dp}}

for all vectors Ydp∈MdpY^{\text{\rm dp}}\in M^{\text{\rm dp}}. The equality of the lemma follows given that the columns of Sdp​(x)S^{\text{\rm dp}}(x) map to 00 under Δdp\Delta^{\text{\rm dp}}. ∎

Remark 4.4.

Hurwitz series provide a framework in which the Picard–Lindelöf (or, Cauchy-Lipschitz) theorem holds for linear differential equations in characteristic pp. The recent article [51] provides another construction allowing this theorem, which has the advantage of yielding an integral domain but which, in return, does not seem so directly linked to the pp-curvature.

4.3 Application to algorithmics

Given that the matrix Sdp​(x)S^{\text{\rm dp}}(x) is invertible, it follows from Lemma 4.3 that one can deduce the value of Bpdp​(x)B_{p}^{\text{\rm dp}}(x) from that of Sdp​(x)S^{\text{\rm dp}}(x) which, in turn, can be computed using the techniques of [17]. However, at this point, we have not solved entirely the question of the computation of the pp-curvature for two reasons. Firstly, the previous reasoning assumes implicitely that the coefficients bi​(x)b_{i}(x)’s have no pole at 00. Secondly, and more importantly, the knowledge of Bpdp​(x)B_{p}^{\text{\rm dp}}(x) is not enough to recover BpB_{p}. Precisely, letting 𝔽p​(x)0\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)_{0} denote the subring of 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x) consisting of functions with no pole at 00, the natural map δ0:𝔽p​(x)0→𝔽p​[[x]]dp\delta_{0}:\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)_{0}\to\mathbb{F}_{p}[[x]]^{\text{\rm dp}} is not injective; its kernel is the ideal generated by xpx^{p}.

To tackle these issues, the idea is to shift around any other base point a∈𝔽pa\in\mathbb{F}_{p}. Doing so, we get a new differential ring homomorphism δa:𝔽p​(x)a→𝔽p​[[x−a]]dp\delta_{a}:\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)_{a}\to\mathbb{F}_{p}[[x{-}a]]^{\text{\rm dp}} and, reusing the same techniques, we end up with a fast algorithm that computes the pp-curvature BpB_{p} modulo (x−a)p(x{-}a)^{p}. Since we have moreover at our disposal a priori bounds on the size of the pp-curvature (see Proposition 4.2), one can pick enough elements aa in 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} (or in a finite extension of 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}, if needed), compute the pp-curvature modulo (x−a)p(x{-}a)^{p} for all those points aa and reconstruct the complete matrix Bp​(x)B_{p}(x) using the Chinese Remainder Theorem. Implementing this strategy, we end up with the following theorem.

Theorem 4.5 (Bostan–Caruso–Schost [15]).

There exists an algorithm that takes as input a differential operator

ℒ=∂xn+bn−1(x)⋅∂xn−1+⋯+b1(x)⋅∂x+b0(x)\mathscr{L}=\partial_{x}^{n}+b_{n-1}(x){\cdot}\partial_{x}^{n-1}+\cdots+b_{1}(x){\cdot}\partial_{x}+b_{0}(x)

over 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x) and outputs its pp-curvature for a cost of O∼​(d​nω​p)O^{\sim}(dn^{\omega}p) operations in 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} with

d=max⁡(deg⁡f⁡(x),deg⁡(f⁡(x)​b0​(x)),…,deg⁡(f⁡(x)​bn−1​(x)))d=\max\big(\deg f(x),\,\deg(f(x)b_{0}(x)),\,\ldots,\,\deg(f(x)b_{n-1}(x))\big)

where f⁡(x)f(x) is a common denominator of the bi​(x)b_{i}(x)’s.

Before commenting on the above result, we need to explain some notation. Firstly, the notation O∼​(−)O^{\sim}(-) means that we are hiding logarithmic factors. Secondly, the exponent ω\omega refers to what we usually call a feasible exponent for the matrix multiplication. It simply means that we suppose that we are given an algorithm that computes the product of two square matrices of size nn using at most O⁡(nω)O(n^{\omega}) operations in the base field. The naive method for multiplying matrices (the one we have all learnt in our first course of linear algebra) indicates that we can take ω=3\omega=3. However, it turns out that better algorithms exist. For example, Strassen’s algorithm [81] results in ω=log2⁡7≈2.8\omega=\log_{2}7\approx 2.8. Nowadays, the best known value for ω\omega is about 2.371882.37188 and the corresponding algorithm is due to Duan, Wu and Zhou [39]. It is a widely open conjecture if one can take ω=2+ε\omega=2+\varepsilon for all ε>0\varepsilon>0.

The announced complexity O∼​(d​nω​p)O^{\sim}(dn^{\omega}p) should be compared to the size of the output, i.e. the number of scalars in 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} needed to write down completely the pp-curvature. By Proposition 4.2, BpB_{p} if an n×nn\times n matrix whose entries are rational functions with numerators and denominators of degree at most d​pdp; in practice, this bound is in general sharp. Therefore, the size of the output is about d​n2​pdn^{2}p. As a consequence, the algorithm behind Theorem 4.5 would be quasi-optimal (i.e. optimal up to constant and logarithmic factors) if ω\omega were equal to 22. Even if this limit cannot be attained, this comparison underlines the good performances of the algorithm. In practice, using it makes it possible to compute pp-curvatures of operators of order and degree 2020 in a few seconds when p<100p<100 and in about half an hour when p=12007p=12007.

4.4 Similarity class and characteristic polynomial

We have seen previously (after Proposition 4.2) that, although the size of the pp-curvature grows linearly with respect to pp, its characteristic polynomial has roughly the same size as the input operator ℒ\mathscr{L} even when pp gets large. For this reason, one might hope to be able to compute the characteristic polynomial faster than the pp-curvature itself.

The main observation for achieving this is a refinement of Lemma 4.3 which asserts that Bpdp​(x)=Bp​(x)​ mod ​xpB_{p}^{\text{\rm dp}}(x)=B_{p}(x)\text{ mod }x^{p} is not only equal to

−(Sdp(x))−1⋅dp​Sdp​(x)d​xp-(S^{\text{\rm dp}}(x))^{-1}\cdot\frac{d^{p}S^{\text{\rm dp}}(x)}{dx^{p}}

but it is further similar to the value at x=0x=0 (i.e. the reduction modulo xx) of the latter product. On the other hand, evaluating this reduction can be done with standard algorithmic techniques (based on a “baby step / giant step” approach) in time proportional to p\sqrt{p}. Based on this, we obtain the next theorem.

Theorem 4.6 (Bostan–Caruso–Schost [16]).

There exists an algorithm that takes as input a differential operator

ℒ=∂xn+bn−1(x)⋅∂xn−1+⋯+b1(x)⋅∂x+b0(x)\mathscr{L}=\partial_{x}^{n}+b_{n-1}(x){\cdot}\partial_{x}^{n-1}+\cdots+b_{1}(x){\cdot}\partial_{x}+b_{0}(x)

over 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x) and outputs the invariant factors of its pp-curvature for a cost of

O∼​(dω+32​nω+1​p)O^{\sim}\big(d^{\omega+\frac{3}{2}}n^{\omega+1}\sqrt{p}\big)

operations in 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} where dd is defined as in Theorem 4.5.

We notice that the knowledge of the invariant factors is finer than that of the characteristic polynomial since the latter is the product of the formers. Furthermore, knowing the invariant factors, one can decide whether the pp-curvature vanishes or not, whereas the characteristic polynomial only gives information about its nilpotency.

On the complexity side, we notice that the cost of the algorithm of Theorem 4.6 is worse with respect to the parameters dd and nn but better with respect to pp. It is then interesting for small operators but large characteristic.

Finally, we mention that, if we are only interested by the characteristic polynomial of the pp-curvature, faster algorithms (based on different techniques) exist.

Theorem 4.7 (Bostan–Caruso–Schost [14]).

There exists an algorithm that takes as input a differential operator

ℒ=∂xn+bn−1(x)⋅∂xn−1+⋯+b1(x)⋅∂x+b0(x)\mathscr{L}=\partial_{x}^{n}+b_{n-1}(x){\cdot}\partial_{x}^{n-1}+\cdots+b_{1}(x){\cdot}\partial_{x}+b_{0}(x)

over 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x) and outputs the characteristic polynomial of its pp-curvature for a cost of

O∼​((d+n)ω​min⁡(d,n)​p+(d+n)ω+1​min⁡(d,n))O^{\sim}\big((d{+}n)^{\omega}\min(d,n)\sqrt{p}+(d{+}n)^{\omega+1}\min(d,n)\big)

operations in 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} where dd is defined as in Theorem 4.5.

In practice, this algorithm performs quite well and allows for computing the characteristic polynomial in less than one hour for the parameters d=n=20d=n=20 and p=120 011p=120\>011.

Recently, Pagès proved an “average version” of this theorem which, roughly speaking, states that, starting with a differential operator over ℚ⁡(x)\mathbb{Q}(x), one can compute all its pp-curvatures (up to some given bound) in average time proportional to log⁡p\log p.

Theorem 4.8 (Pagès [70]).

There exists an algorithm that takes as input a differential operator

ℒ=bn(x)⋅∂xn+bn−1(x)⋅∂xn−1+⋯+b1(x)⋅∂x+b0(x)\mathscr{L}=b_{n}(x)\cdot\partial_{x}^{n}+b_{n-1}(x){\cdot}\partial_{x}^{n-1}+\cdots+b_{1}(x){\cdot}\partial_{x}+b_{0}(x)

with bi​(x)∈ℤ​[x]b_{i}(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x] and outputs the characteristic polynomial of all the pp-curvatures of ℒ​ mod ​p\mathscr{L}\text{ mod }p for p≤Np\leq N for a cost of

O∼​(((d+n)ω​(d+m)+(d+n)3)⋅N​d)O^{\sim}\big(\big((d{+}n)^{\omega}(d{+}m)+(d{+}n)^{3}\big)\cdot Nd\big)

operations on bits, where dd is the maximal degree of the bi​(x)b_{i}(x)’s and mm is the maximal bitsize of an integer appearing as the coefficient of one of the bi​(x)b_{i}(x)’s.

5 Algebraicity and integrality

The theoretical developments we carried out in §4.2 have also interesting consequences in characteristic 00, as they allow to relate algebraicity of solutions with the growth of denominators of the coefficients in their Taylor expansions. The aim of this section is to appetize the reader with some charming results and perspectives in this direction.

Throughout this section, we let

ℒ=∂xn+bn−1(x)⋅∂xn−1+⋯+b1(x)⋅∂x+b0(x)\mathscr{L}=\partial_{x}^{n}+b_{n-1}(x){\cdot}\partial_{x}^{n-1}+\cdots+b_{1}(x){\cdot}\partial_{x}+b_{0}(x)

be a differential operator over ℚ⁡(x)\mathbb{Q}(x) and assume that bi​(x)b_{i}(x) has no pole at 00 for all ii. We set:

S⁡(x)=∑k=0∞(−1)k​Bk​(x)⋅xkk!S(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{k}B_{k}(x)\cdot\frac{x^{k}}{k!} (30)

where the Bk​(x)B_{k}(x)’s are defined by equation (28). The matrix S⁡(x)S(x) has entries in ℚ⁡[[x]]\mathbb{Q}[[x]] and we write S⁡(x)=∑i=0∞Si​xiS(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}S_{i}x^{i} where the SiS_{i} are matrices over ℚ\mathbb{Q}. We emphasize that SiS_{i} is not equal to (−1)ii!​Bi​(x)\frac{(-1)^{i}}{i!}B_{i}(x) because the latter has in general coefficients in ℚ⁡(x)\mathbb{Q}(x).

5.1 Growth of denominators and pp-curvatures

We would like to compare S⁡(x)S(x) with the matrix Sdp​(x)S^{\text{\rm dp}}(x) introduced in equation (29) and, for this, to reduce everything (ℒ\mathscr{L}, S⁡(x)S(x), etc.) modulo a prime number pp. However, this operation requires some care because the Bk​(x)B_{k}(x)’s may exhibit denominators. In order to do it properly, we introduce new rings. For any subring R⊂ℚR\subset\mathbb{Q}, we set:

R⁡(x)\displaystyle R(x) ={PQwithP,Q∈R⁡[x]​ and ​Q​ monic},\displaystyle=\left\{\,\frac{P}{Q}\quad\text{with}\quad P,Q\in R[x]\text{ and }Q\text{ monic}\,\right\},
R​(x)0\displaystyle R(x)_{0} ={PQwithP,Q∈R⁡[x],Q​ monic and ​Q​(0)≠0},\displaystyle=\left\{\,\frac{P}{Q}\quad\text{with}\quad P,Q\in R[x],\,Q\text{ monic}\text{ and }Q(0)\neq 0\,\right\},
R​[[x]]dp\displaystyle R[[x]]^{\text{\rm dp}} ={∑i=0∞ai​xii!withai∈R​ for all ​i}.\displaystyle=\left\{\,\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}a_{i}\>\frac{x^{i}}{i!}\quad\text{with}\quad a_{i}\in R\text{ for all }i\,\right\}.

One has the following chain of inclusions R⁡[x]⊂R​(x)0⊂R⁡(x)R[x]\subset R(x)_{0}\subset R(x) together with an injective morphism of rings R​(x)0↪R⁡[[x]]R(x)_{0}\hookrightarrow R[[x]]. Besides, all these maps commute with the derivation dd​x\frac{d}{dx} and, if pp is a prime number which is noninvertible in RR, they are compatible with the reduction modulo pp; in particular, we have the following commutative diagram:

where all the arrows are homomorphisms of rings and commute with the derivation. We now assume that the entries of B⁡(x)B(x) have no pole at 00 and choose RR in such a way that they all belong to R​(x)0R(x)_{0} (one can always take R=ℤ⁡[1D]R=\mathbb{Z}[\frac{1}{D}] for DD large enough). All the Bm​(x)B_{m}(x)’s then take coefficients in R​(x)0R(x)_{0} as well and the matrix S⁡(x)S(x) is defined over R​[[x]]dpR[[x]]^{\text{\rm dp}}. Besides, the image of S⁡(x)S(x) modulo pp is the matrix Sdp​(x)S^{\text{\rm dp}}(x) modulo pp associated to the differential system Y′+(B⁡(x)​mod​p)⋅Y=0Y^{\prime}+(B(x)\,\text{\rm mod}\,p)\cdot Y=0 in characteristic pp. Lemma 4.3 then leaves us with the congruence:

Sp≡Bp​(x)p!(modx),i.e.Sp=Bp​(0)p!.S_{p}\equiv\frac{B_{p}(x)}{p!}\pmod{x},\quad\text{i.e.}\quad S_{p}=\frac{B_{p}(0)}{p!}. (31)

Hence the pp-curvatures (which, we recall, are the matrices Bp​(x)​mod​pB_{p}(x)\,\text{\rm mod}\,p) are directly related to the coefficients appearing in a fundamental system of solutions. In particular, the vanishing of Bp​(0)B_{p}(0) modulo pp is equivalent to the fact that the denominator of SpS_{p} is coprime with pp. Many variations on this theme are possible; a beautiful example is given by the following theorem.

Theorem 5.1 (see Proposition 5.3.3 in [5]).

Let

ℒ=∂xn+bn−1(x)⋅∂xn−1+⋯+b1(x)⋅∂x+b0(x)\mathscr{L}=\partial_{x}^{n}+b_{n-1}(x){\cdot}\partial_{x}^{n-1}+\cdots+b_{1}(x){\cdot}\partial_{x}+b_{0}(x)

be a differential operator over ℚ⁡(x)\mathbb{Q}(x) and DD be a positive integer. We assume that ℒ\mathscr{L} admits nn solutions Y1,…,YnY_{1},\ldots,Y_{n} which have coordinates in ℤ​[1D]​[[x]]\mathbb{Z}[\frac{1}{D}][[x]] and are linearly independent over ℚ\mathbb{Q}. Then almost all the pp-curvatures of ℒ\mathscr{L} vanish.

Remark 5.2.

Under Grothendieck’s conjecture, Theorem 5.1 can be elegantly rephrased as follows: if a differential system admits a basis of solutions in ℤ​[1D]​[[x]]\mathbb{Z}[\frac{1}{D}][[x]] for some positive integer DD (i.e., a basis of globally bounded solutions), then it also admits a basis of algebraic solutions. This is known as Bézivin’s conjecture; it was formulated by Bézivin in [11, p. 299] and proved by him for qq-differential equations [11, Thm. 7-1]; see also Conjecture 6.3 in [30]. It is widely open whether Bézivin’s conjecture is more difficult than Grothendieck’s conjecture; at any rate, it appears that for the time being the only cases for which Bézivin’s conjecture is proven are those for which Grothendieck’s conjecture is known to be true.

Example 5.3.

We illustrate Theorem 5.1 with the differential equation

y′=1x2+1​yy^{\prime}=\frac{1}{x^{2}+1}y

already considered in Example 3.4. Over the rationals, the solutions are all proportional to the fundamental solution

y0​(x)=exp⁡(arctan⁡(x))=∑n=0∞cn​xny_{0}(x)=\exp(\arctan(x))=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_{n}x^{n}

where the cnc_{n}’s are rational numbers. We would like to find bounds on denominators of the cnc_{n}’s. More precisely, we fix a prime number p≠2p\neq 2 (for simplicity) and ask whether the denominators of the cnc_{n}’s are all coprime with pp. For this, we use the following important result due to Dwork.

Theorem 5.4 (Dwork’s criterion, [75, p. 409]).

Given a prime pp and f⁡(x)∈x​ℚ​[[x]]f(x)\in x\mathbb{Q}[[x]], we have exp⁡(f⁡(x))∈1+x​ℤ(p)​[[x]]\exp(f(x))\in 1+x\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}[[x]] if and only if f⁡(xp)−p​f​(x)∈p​x​ℤ(p)​[[x]]f(x^{p})-pf(x)\in px\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}[[x]], where ℤ(p)\mathbb{Z}_{(p)} is the subring of ℚ\mathbb{Q} consisting of fractions ab\frac{a}{b} with bb coprime with pp.

According to Dwork’s criterion, the denominators of the cnc_{n}’s are all coprime with pp if and only if

arctan⁡(xp)−p⋅arctan⁡(x)∈p​ℤ(p)​[[x]].\arctan(x^{p})-p\cdot\arctan(x)\in p\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}[[x]].

We have:

arctan⁡(xp)−p⋅arctan⁡(x)=∑n=0∞(−1)n2​n+1​x(2​n+1)​p−p⋅∑n=0∞(−1)n2​n+1​x(2​n+1).\arctan(x^{p})-p\cdot\arctan(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n}}{2n+1}x^{(2n+1)p}-p\cdot\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n}}{2n+1}x^{(2n+1)}. (32)

Clearly, when 2​n+12n+1 is coprime with pp, the coefficient p⋅(−1)n2​n+1p\cdot\frac{(-1)^{n}}{2n+1} is divisible by pp. Therefore, we can only retain in the second sum of equation (32) the terms for which 2​n≡−1(modp)2n\equiv-1\pmod{p}, i.e. 2​n=p−1+2​ℓ​p2n=p-1+2\ell p with ℓ∈ℕ\ell\in\mathbb{N}. We thus get:

arctan⁡(xp)−p⋅arctan⁡(x)\displaystyle\arctan(x^{p})-p\cdot\arctan(x) ≡∑n=0∞(−1)n2​n+1​x(2​n+1)​p−∑ℓ=0∞(−1)ℓ−p−122​ℓ+1​x(2​ℓ+1)​p\displaystyle\equiv\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n}}{2n+1}x^{(2n+1)p}-\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{\ell-\frac{p-1}{2}}}{2\ell+1}x^{(2\ell+1)p}
=∑n=0∞(−1)n2​n+1⋅(1−(−1)p−12)⋅x(2​n+1)​p(modp​ℤ(p)​[[x]]),\displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n}}{2n+1}\cdot\left(1-(-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}}\right)\cdot x^{(2n+1)p}\pmod{p\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}[[x]]},

hence arctan⁡(xp)−p⋅arctan⁡(x)\arctan(x^{p})-p\cdot\arctan(x) is divisible by pp when p≡1​mod​ 4p\equiv 1\,\text{\rm mod}\,4 and is not otherwise. In conclusion, the denominators of the cnc_{n}’s are all coprime with pp (that is, exp⁡(arctan⁡(x))\exp(\arctan(x)) can be reduced modulo pp) if and only if p≡1​mod​ 4p\equiv 1\,\text{\rm mod}\,4.

Remark 5.5.

Note that the sequence (Tn)n≥0(T_{n})_{n\geq 0} defined by Tn=n!⋅cnT_{n}=n!\cdot c_{n}, satisfies the linear recurrence Tn+2=Tn+1−n⁡(n+1)​TnT_{n+2}=T_{n+1}-n(n+1)T_{n} with T0=T1=1T_{0}=T_{1}=1, hence its terms are all integer numbers. Kelinsky proved in [61, Thm. 3] that for any prime p≠2p\neq 2, the term TpT_{p} is congruent to 00 modulo pp if p≡1​mod​ 4p\equiv 1\,\text{\rm mod}\,4 (and to 22 if p≡3​mod​ 4p\equiv 3\,\text{\rm mod}\,4). The computation in Example 5.3 provides a new proof of this statement: if p≡1​mod​ 4p\equiv 1\,\text{\rm mod}\,4, then TnT_{n} is congruent to 00 modulo pp for all n≥pn\geq p, in other terms the generating function ∑n≥0Tn​xn\sum_{n\geq 0}T_{n}x^{n} is a polynomial modulo pp.

In the same orbit, we mention two other theorems which are not directly related to our discussion but highlights other intricate relations between algebraicity and integrality.

Theorem 5.6 (Conjectured by Ogus [69], proved by André [4]).

Let f⁡(x)∈ℤ⁡[[x]]f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[[x]] such that f′​(x)f^{\prime}(x) is algebraic over ℚ⁡(x)\mathbb{Q}(x). Then f⁡(x)f(x) is algebraic over ℚ⁡(x)\mathbb{Q}(x).

Theorem 5.7 (Conjectured by Katz [55], proved by the Chudnovsky–Chudnovsky [35]).

Let f⁡(x)∈ℤ⁡[[x]]f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[[x]] such that f′​(x)/f​(x)f^{\prime}(x)/f(x) is algebraic over ℚ⁡(x)\mathbb{Q}(x). Then f⁡(x)f(x) is algebraic over ℚ⁡(x)\mathbb{Q}(x).

5.2 An analytic perspective on the pp-curvature

All that precedes indicates that the vanishing properties of the pp-curvatures tend to control the growth of the denominators of the coefficients of the fundamental system of solutions S⁡(x)S(x). Typically, after equation (31), we have seen that Bp​(0)≡0(modp)B_{p}(0)\equiv 0\pmod{p} is equivalent to the fact that pp does not divide the smallest common denominator of the entries of SpS_{p}.

It is convenient to reformulate this class of properties in terms of pp-adic valuation and pp-adic numbers. We recall that the pp-adic valuation of an integer nn, denoted by vp​(n)v_{p}(n), is the greatest integer vv such that pvp^{v} divides nn. We then define the pp-adic valuation of a rational number x=abx=\frac{a}{b} by setting vp​(x)=vp​(a)−vp​(b)v_{p}(x)=v_{p}(a)-v_{p}(b). Having a denominator coprime with pp is then equivalent to having nonnegative pp-adic valuation. If MM is a matrix over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, we define vp​(M)v_{p}(M) as the minimum of the pp-valuations of its entries.

Recall that, for all nonnegative integer ii, we have:

vp​(i!)=∑n=1∞⌊ipn⌋≤ip−1v_{p}(i!)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left\lfloor\frac{i}{p^{n}}\right\rfloor\leq\frac{i}{p-1}

(where ⌊⋅⌋\lfloor\,\cdot\,\rfloor is the floor function). Hence, if S⁡(x)S(x) is defined over ℤ​[1D]​[[x]]\mathbb{Z}[\frac{1}{D}][[x]] and pp is a prime number which does not divide NN, we deduce from the very first definition of S⁡(x)S(x) (see equation (30)) that vp​(Si)≥−vp​(i!)≥−ip−1v_{p}(S_{i})\geq-v_{p}(i!)\geq\frac{-i}{p{-}1} for all ii. On the other hand, the property we have recalled above indicates that Bp​(0)≡0(modp)B_{p}(0)\equiv 0\pmod{p} if and only if vp​(Sp)≥0v_{p}(S_{p})\geq 0. It turns out actually that the vanishing of the pp-curvature implies a general lower bound on the pp-adic valuation of the SiS_{i}’s.

Proposition 5.8.

Let

ℒ=∂xn+bn−1(x)⋅∂xn−1+⋯+b1(x)⋅∂x+b0(x)\mathscr{L}=\partial_{x}^{n}+b_{n-1}(x){\cdot}\partial_{x}^{n-1}+\cdots+b_{1}(x){\cdot}\partial_{x}+b_{0}(x)

be a differential operator over ℚ⁡(x)\mathbb{Q}(x) and let SS be the matrix defined by equation (30). If the reduction of ℒ\mathscr{L} modulo p is well-defined and if the pp-curvature of ℒ​ mod ​p\mathscr{L}\text{ mod }p vanishes, then for all i≥0i\geq 0:

vp​(Si)≥−vp​(⌊i/p⌋!)≥−ip⁡(p−1).v_{p}(S_{i})\geq-v_{p}\big(\lfloor i/p\rfloor!\big)\geq\frac{-i}{p(p{-}1)}. (33)

Proposition 5.8 can be further rephrased in more analytic terms using pp-adic numbers. We recall briefly that the field of pp-adic numbers is the completion of ℚ\mathbb{Q} for the pp-adic norm ∥⋅∥p\|\cdot\|_{p} defined by ‖x‖p=p−vp​(x)\|x\|_{p}=p^{-v_{p}(x)}. Set ω=p−1/(p−1)\omega=p^{-1/(p-1)}. Without any assumption on the pp-curvature, we have seen that vp​(Si)≥−ip−1v_{p}(S_{i})\geq\frac{-i}{p-1}, that is ‖Si‖p≤ω−i\|S_{i}\|_{p}\leq\omega^{-i}. This upper bound indicates that the (pp-adic) radius of convergence of the series S⁡(x)=∑i=0∞Si​xiS(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}S_{i}x^{i} is at least ω\omega. On the contrary, when the pp-curvature vanishes, Proposition 5.8 tells us that ∥Si∥p≤ω−i/p\|S_{i}\|_{p}\leq\omega^{-i/p} for all ii. Hence, the radius of convergence of SS is now at least ω1/p>ω\omega^{1/p}>\omega. The pp-curvature then measures some analytic properties of the solutions of our differential system in the pp-adic world. A classical result in the theory of pp-adic differential equations [60, Theorem 10.4.2], refining the Frobenius antecedent theorem of Christol and Dwork [34, Thm. 5.4] (see also [59, Theorem 6.15]), asserts that when the radius of convergence of a fundamental system of solutions is strictly greater than ω\omega, the corresponding differential system Y′​(x)+B⁡(x)​Y​(x)=0Y^{\prime}(x)+B(x)Y(x)=0 is equivalent, up to a base change, to a system of the form Y′​(xp)+C⁡(xp)​Y​(xp)=0Y^{\prime}(x^{p})+C(x^{p})Y(x^{p})=0 where the entries of C⁡(x)C(x) are pp-adic analytic functions converging on the closed unit disk. The differential system:

(Σ1):Y′+C⁡(x)​Y=0(\Sigma_{1}):Y^{\prime}+C(x)Y=0

is called a Frobenius antecedent of (Σ)(\Sigma). The aforementioned convergence conditions allow for reducing (Σ1)(\Sigma_{1}) modulo pp, thus obtaining a new differential system on 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x). The latter has a well-defined pp-curvature and if this second pp-curvature persists to vanish, one eventually deduces that the radius of convergence of SS is at least ω1/p2\omega^{1/p^{2}}. When this occurs, one can continue this process and find a second Frobenius antecedent (Σ2)(\Sigma_{2}) of (Σ)(\Sigma). If its pp-curvature vanishes, the radius of convergence of SS will be at least ω1/p3\omega^{1/p^{3}} and so on and so forth.

In the perspective of the Grothendieck conjecture, we would like to let pp vary and understand how the aforementioned convergence properties interact. A promising object, which looks capable to reflect these interactions is the Berkovich line over ℤ\mathbb{Z}, which was anticipated by Berkovich himself in [6] and then developed by Poineau [72]. By definition, it is the space ℳ⁡(ℤ⁡[x])\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}[x]) consisting of all bounded multiplicative semi-norms ∥⋅∥:ℤ[x]→ℝ\|\cdot\|:\mathbb{Z}[x]\to\mathbb{R}. A semi-norm is a norm except that we authorize nonzero elements to have norm zero. It is said multiplicative if ‖f​g‖=‖f‖⋅‖g‖\|fg\|=\|f\|\cdot\|g\| for all f,g∈ℤ⁡[x]f,g\in\mathbb{Z}[x] and bounded when

‖a0+a1​x+⋯+an​xn‖≤max⁡(|a0|,|a1|,…,|an|),\|a_{0}+a_{1}x+\cdots+a_{n}x^{n}\|\leq\max\big(|a_{0}|,|a_{1}|,\ldots,|a_{n}|\big),

where |ai||a_{i}| denotes the usual absolute value of aia_{i}. Of course, the Berkovich line ℳ⁡(ℤ⁡[x])\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}[x]) is not only a set but is endowed with a rich additional geometrical structure: a topology, a structural sheaf, etc. Besides, after Poineau’s work, we have at our disposal a whole panel of powerful tools (inspired by modern algebraic geometry) to work with it.

Describing entirely the space ℳ⁡(ℤ⁡[x])\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}[x]) is not obvious, but it is not difficult to exhibit elements in it. Take K=ℝK=\mathbb{R} or ℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p} (the field of pp-adic numbers) for some prime number pp and write ∥⋅∥K\|\cdot\|_{K} for the standard absolute value of KK. Pick in addition an element a∈Ka\in K of norm at most 11 and a nonnegative real number rr. Polynomials in ℤ⁡[x]\mathbb{Z}[x] then define (real or pp-adic) analytic functions on the closed ball B⁡(a,r)B(a,r) of center aa and radius rr. For f∈ℤ⁡[x]f\in\mathbb{Z}[x], we can then consider the sup norm on this domain:

‖f‖a,r=supx∈B⁡(a,r)‖f⁡(x)‖K.\|f\|_{a,r}=\sup_{x\in B(a,r)}\|f(x)\|_{K}.

One checks that it is an element of ℳ⁡(ℤ⁡[x])\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}[x]). Moreover, at least in the pp-adic case, the completion of ℤ⁡[x]\mathbb{Z}[x] with respect to this norm is the ring of pp-adic analytic functions on B⁡(a,r)B(a,r); we shall denote it by 𝒜a,r\mathcal{A}_{a,r} in what follows. Another nice observation is that the notion of “ball of center aa and radius rr” has a well-defined meaning in the Berkovich geometry. Indeed, let ℳ⁡(𝒜a,r)\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{A}_{a,r}) be the Berkovich space associated to the ring 𝒜a,r\mathcal{A}_{a,r}, i.e. the set of bounded multiplicative semi-norms on 𝒜a,r\mathcal{A}_{a,r}. Restricting a semi-norm from 𝒜a,r\mathcal{A}_{a,r} to ℤ⁡[x]\mathbb{Z}[x] leaves us with an injective map:

ℳ⁡(𝒜a,r)↪ℳ⁡(ℤ⁡[x])\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{A}_{a,r})\hookrightarrow\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}[x])

whose image, denoted by Ua,rU_{a,r}, is an open subset (for the Berkovich topology) in ℳ⁡(ℤ⁡[x])\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}[x]). In addition, we observe that any analytic function ff on B⁡(a,r)B(a,r), that is any element f∈𝒜a,rf\in\mathcal{A}_{a,r}, induces a function on Ua,rU_{a,r}: to each semi-norm ∥⋅∥∈ℳ(𝒜a,r)\|\cdot\|\in\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{A}_{a,r}), we associate ‖f‖\|f\|. For this reason, it is natural to think at Ua,rU_{a,r} as the Berkovich incarnation of the ball of center aa and radius rr.

Coming back to our topic, let us consider a differential system (Σ):Y′+A⁡(x)​Y=0(\Sigma):Y^{\prime}+A(x)Y=0 over ℤ⁡[x]\mathbb{Z}[x]. By what we have seen previously, for almost all prime numbers pp and all a∈ℤpa\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}, the system (Σ)(\Sigma) admits a full basis of solutions in 𝒜a,ω\mathcal{A}_{a,\omega} where we recall that we have set ω=p−1/(p−1)\omega=p^{-1/(p-1)}. In the Berkovich language, these functions give rise to new functions defined on Ua,ωU_{a,\omega}. Putting them together, we conclude that (Σ)(\Sigma) always admits a basis of solutions on a certain open subspace U0⊂ℳ⁡(ℤ⁡[x])U_{0}\subset\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}[x]). Now, the assumption that almost all the pp-curvatures vanish shows that those solutions extend automatically to a larger subspace U1⊂ℳ⁡(ℤ⁡[x])U_{1}\subset\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}[x]). On the other hand, in the Berkovich language, proving the Grothendieck conjecture amounts to showing that there exist a full basis of solution on an étale covering of ℳ⁡(ℤ⁡[x])\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}[x]). Of course, these remarks do not give any proof of the Grothendieck conjecture because U1U_{1} itself is certainly not an étale covering of ℳ⁡(ℤ⁡[x])\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}[x]). However, we think that this point of view has the potential to lead to new interesting developments towards the Grothendieck conjecture in the future.
